name: Coagulative necrosis
definition: Irreversible tissue death with temporary preservation of the basic tissue framework.
pathogenesis: Ischemia causes ATP depletion, membrane injury and enzyme dysfunction. Protein denaturation delays digestion of the dead cells.
gross: Pale, firm infarct in many solid organs
A wedge-shaped lesion may point toward an occluded vessel
microscopy: Eosinophilic anucleate ghost cells
Preserved tissue outlines early
Inflammation develops around the infarct
clinical: Seen in myocardial, renal and splenic infarcts
Appearance changes with lesion age
examTips: Most ischemic infarcts outside the brain show this pattern.

differentials.name: Liquefactive necrosis
differentials.distinction: Tissue architecture is digested rather than preserved.

name: Liquefactive necrosis
definition: Tissue death in which enzymatic digestion converts the affected tissue into a soft liquid mass.
pathogenesis: Hydrolytic enzymes digest dead cells faster than the tissue framework can persist. Neutrophil enzymes dominate in abscesses, while ischemic brain injury also follows this pattern.
gross: Soft or liquid necrotic centre
An old brain infarct may leave a cystic cavity
microscopy: Loss of recognizable tissue architecture
Necrotic debris and macrophages
Numerous neutrophils in a pyogenic abscess
clinical: Typical of abscesses and cerebral infarction
Infection and sterile brain ischemia require different clinical interpretation
examTips: Liquefaction describes morphology, not proof of infection.

differentials.name: Coagulative necrosis
differentials.distinction: Retains ghost outlines, especially early.

name: Caseous necrosis
definition: A friable form of necrosis classically associated with necrotizing granulomatous inflammation.
pathogenesis: Cell-mediated responses to persistent organisms can generate granulomas with central tissue destruction. Tuberculosis is a major cause, but fungal infections can produce a similar pattern.
gross: Soft white-yellow material resembling crumbled cheese
May occupy the centre of a granuloma
microscopy: Amorphous granular eosinophilic debris
Loss of cell outlines
Epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells may surround the necrosis
clinical: Often associated with tuberculosis
A negative acid-fast stain does not exclude tuberculosis
examTips: Caseation suggests a differential; demonstrate the cause where possible.

differentials.name: Non-necrotizing granuloma
differentials.distinction: Has no central caseous debris; sarcoidosis is one consideration.

stains: Ziehl–Neelsen for acid-fast organisms; sensitivity is limited
GMS or PAS when fungi are suspected

name: Fat necrosis
definition: Death of adipocytes with a reactive inflammatory response and sometimes calcium deposition.
pathogenesis: In pancreatitis, released lipases hydrolyse triglycerides and liberated fatty acids bind calcium. Trauma can also injure adipose tissue, particularly in the breast.
gross: Chalky white deposits in pancreatic or peripancreatic fat
An injured breast may contain a firm irregular lesion
microscopy: Ghost outlines of dead adipocytes
Basophilic calcium soaps may form
Foamy macrophages and foreign-body giant cells in older lesions
clinical: Can accompany acute pancreatitis
Breast fat necrosis can mimic carcinoma clinically or radiologically
examTips: Link the chalky deposits to saponification in enzymatic fat necrosis.

differentials.name: Lipoma
differentials.distinction: A benign mass of viable mature adipocytes without the necrotic inflammatory reaction.

name: Fibrinoid necrosis
definition: A microscopic pattern of vascular injury with intensely eosinophilic material in vessel walls.
pathogenesis: Severe vascular injury permits plasma proteins, including fibrin, to enter the damaged wall. Immune-mediated vasculitis and severe hypertension are important settings.
gross: Usually recognized microscopically rather than as a separate gross lesion
Gross changes reflect the affected organ or underlying vascular disease
microscopy: Bright pink vessel-wall material
Wall necrosis and loss of normal detail
Inflammatory cells may accompany immune-mediated injury
clinical: May occur in necrotizing vasculitis
Can accompany severe hypertension
examTips: Do not confuse fibrinoid vascular injury with amyloid solely because both look pink on H&E.

differentials.name: Amyloid
differentials.distinction: Extracellular deposits are Congo-red positive with characteristic birefringence.

stains: Congo red when amyloid is in the differential

name: Amyloidosis
definition: Extracellular accumulation of misfolded proteins arranged as insoluble fibrils.
pathogenesis: Different precursor proteins can form a similar fibrillar architecture. AL, AA and transthyretin-associated forms have different underlying causes, so identifying the deposited protein matters.
gross: Organs may be enlarged, firm or waxy
Distribution varies with amyloid type and site
microscopy: Extracellular amorphous eosinophilic deposits
Vascular and parenchymal deposition may coexist
Fine nonbranching fibrils on electron microscopy
clinical: Renal deposition can cause proteinuria
Cardiac involvement can produce a restrictive phenotype
examTips: Congo red establishes amyloid; it does not establish the precursor protein type.

differentials.name: Hyaline collagen
differentials.distinction: May also look pink but lacks the characteristic Congo-red staining pattern.

stains: Congo red with apple-green birefringence under polarized light

name: Atherosclerosis
definition: Intimal plaques containing lipid, inflammatory cells and fibrous tissue in large and medium arteries.
pathogenesis: Lipid retention and endothelial dysfunction recruit monocytes into the intima. Inflammation and smooth-muscle matrix deposition build a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich core.
gross: Raised yellow-white intimal plaques
Complicated plaques may ulcerate, calcify or develop overlying thrombus
microscopy: Fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core
Foam cells and cholesterol clefts
Variable calcification, inflammation and luminal narrowing
clinical: Can cause coronary, cerebral or peripheral ischemia
Plaque disruption can precipitate acute thrombosis
examTips: Distinguish chronic luminal narrowing from acute plaque rupture and thrombosis.

differentials.name: Medial calcific sclerosis
differentials.distinction: Calcification is primarily medial and need not cause major luminal narrowing.

stains: Elastic stains help assess vessel-wall architecture

name: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
definition: Concentric thickening of small arterial or arteriolar walls that narrows the lumen.
pathogenesis: Severe vascular stress, classically associated with marked hypertension, drives concentric cellular and matrix accumulation. The narrowed lumen worsens downstream ischemia.
gross: Usually part of organ damage rather than a discrete gross mass
Renal cortical ischemic change may coexist
microscopy: Concentric laminated wall thickening
Marked luminal narrowing
Fibrinoid injury may coexist in severe cases
clinical: Associated with severe hypertension
May also occur in thrombotic microangiopathy and other vascular disorders
examTips: The onion-skin pattern is a morphology, not a diagnosis of hypertension in isolation.

differentials.name: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
differentials.distinction: Shows homogeneous pink wall thickening rather than prominent concentric lamination.

name: Myocardial infarction
definition: Ischemic death of cardiac muscle, most often caused by acute coronary thrombosis.
pathogenesis: A disrupted atherosclerotic plaque can trigger coronary occlusion. Prolonged loss of perfusion causes irreversible myocyte injury followed by inflammation and scar formation.
gross: Early changes can be subtle
Later pallor and softening give way to a firm scar
microscopy: Coagulative myocyte necrosis with nuclear loss
Neutrophils followed by macrophages as the lesion evolves
Granulation tissue and collagen in healing lesions
clinical: Acute chest pain and biomarker elevation require clinical correlation
Complications include arrhythmia, rupture and ventricular dysfunction
examTips: Histological timing is approximate and affected by reperfusion and sampling.

differentials.name: Myocarditis
differentials.distinction: Inflammatory injury need not follow a coronary vascular territory.

name: Rheumatic heart disease
definition: Immune-mediated cardiac injury following infection with group A streptococci, with chronic valvular scarring in some patients.
pathogenesis: Cross-reactive immune responses can injure cardiac tissues after streptococcal infection. Recurrent inflammation promotes leaflet fibrosis, commissural fusion and chordal shortening.
gross: Chronic mitral disease may produce a narrowed fish-mouth orifice
Leaflets and chordae become thickened and distorted
microscopy: Aschoff bodies can occur in active rheumatic carditis
Activated histiocytes may have wavy caterpillar-like chromatin
Chronic valves show fibrosis, neovascularization and calcification
clinical: May cause mitral stenosis or regurgitation
Atrial enlargement increases risks of atrial fibrillation and embolism
examTips: Aschoff bodies indicate rheumatic inflammation; a chronic scarred valve may not contain them.

differentials.name: Infective endocarditis
differentials.distinction: Typically has friable infected vegetations and destructive inflammation rather than isolated chronic commissural fusion.

name: Infective endocarditis
definition: Microbial infection of an endocardial surface, usually a cardiac valve.
pathogenesis: Blood-borne organisms colonize a susceptible surface or directly invade previously normal tissue. Infected thrombotic vegetations can damage the valve and shed septic emboli.
gross: Bulky friable valve vegetations
Valve perforation or a ring abscess may complicate infection
microscopy: Fibrin and platelet vegetations
Organisms may be embedded in necrotic debris
Acute inflammation and tissue destruction vary with the organism and treatment
clinical: Fever, bacteremia and embolic phenomena are important clues
Negative tissue stains do not exclude partially treated infection
examTips: Correlate morphology with cultures and other microbiology rather than naming the organism from H&E alone.

differentials.name: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis
differentials.distinction: Sterile vegetations typically lack organisms and marked destructive inflammation.

stains: Gram stain for bacteria
GMS or PAS for selected fungal differentials

name: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
definition: A usually inherited myocardial disorder characterized by otherwise unexplained hypertrophy and abnormal myocyte organization.
pathogenesis: Many cases involve sarcomeric protein variants. Disordered muscle growth and small-vessel abnormalities impair relaxation and can contribute to ischemia and arrhythmia.
gross: A thickened ventricular wall, often with asymmetric septal hypertrophy
The ventricular cavity can be small
microscopy: Enlarged myocytes with hypertrophic nuclei
Myocyte disarray, best judged in context
Interstitial fibrosis and small intramural arterial changes may coexist
clinical: May present with exertional symptoms or sudden death
Left ventricular outflow obstruction occurs in a subset
examTips: Disarray alone is not sufficient; small foci can occur at normal ventricular junctions.

differentials.name: Hypertensive hypertrophy
differentials.distinction: Often has more orderly myocyte enlargement and requires clinical blood-pressure correlation.

stains: Trichrome highlights fibrosis

name: Dilated cardiomyopathy
definition: A myocardial phenotype with ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction not explained solely by abnormal loading or coronary disease.
pathogenesis: Genetic disease, toxins, myocarditis and metabolic injury can converge on impaired contractility. Progressive chamber enlargement increases wall stress and predisposes to mural thrombosis.
gross: An enlarged heart with dilated chambers
Mural thrombi may be present
microscopy: Hypertrophied and attenuated myocytes
Variable interstitial fibrosis
No single microscopic feature establishes the underlying cause
clinical: Can cause congestive heart failure and arrhythmia
The clinical work-up determines the etiology
examTips: Dilated cardiomyopathy is a phenotype, not one histologically uniform disease.

differentials.name: Ischemic cardiomyopathy
differentials.distinction: Requires assessment for coronary disease and ischemic scars in the appropriate distribution.

stains: Trichrome highlights interstitial and replacement fibrosis

name: Emphysema
definition: Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles with destruction of alveolar walls.
pathogenesis: Protease–antiprotease imbalance and oxidative injury promote loss of elastic tissue. Smoking and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency produce different characteristic distributions.
gross: Hyperinflated lungs
Bullae can form in advanced disease
microscopy: Enlarged airspaces with thinned or absent septa
Reduced alveolar capillary bed
Inflammation and fibrosis are variable rather than defining features
clinical: Contributes to airflow obstruction and reduced gas exchange
Bullous disease can predispose to pneumothorax
examTips: Centrilobular disease classically relates to smoking; panacinar disease raises alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

differentials.name: Honeycomb fibrosis
differentials.distinction: Cystic spaces are accompanied by established interstitial scarring rather than predominantly septal destruction.

name: Bronchiectasis
definition: Permanent dilation of bronchi and bronchioles caused by destruction of their walls.
pathogenesis: Persistent infection or obstruction sustains inflammation and impairs clearance. Repeated injury destroys bronchial smooth muscle and elastic tissue, creating a self-perpetuating cycle.
gross: Dilated airways can extend close to the pleural surface
Lumens may contain purulent material
microscopy: Airway-wall inflammation and destruction
Ulceration and squamous metaplasia may occur
Fibrosis surrounds chronically injured airways
clinical: Associated with recurrent productive infections and hemoptysis
Underlying causes include obstruction, cystic fibrosis and impaired ciliary function
examTips: The defining lesion is irreversible airway dilation, not simply mucus in an airway.

differentials.name: Chronic bronchitis
differentials.distinction: Mucus hypersecretion does not by itself establish destructive permanent bronchial dilation.

name: Lobar pneumonia
definition: An acute pneumonic pattern with confluent consolidation of a large part of a lobe.
pathogenesis: An infectious process spreads through adjacent alveoli. Alveolar exudation impairs ventilation and can progress through overlapping congestive and hepatization phases.
gross: A consolidated, firm airless lobe
The cut surface may be red or grey depending on stage
microscopy: Alveoli filled by neutrophils and fibrin
Red cells may be prominent early
Resolution involves macrophage clearance of exudate
clinical: May present with fever, cough and pleuritic pain
Complications include pleuritis, abscess or organization
examTips: The classic stages overlap; a specimen need not show the entire textbook sequence.

differentials.name: Bronchopneumonia
differentials.distinction: Usually has a patchy bronchiolocentric distribution rather than confluent lobar involvement.

stains: Gram stain may demonstrate bacteria, but culture is needed for organism identification

name: Bronchopneumonia
definition: Patchy acute suppurative inflammation centred on bronchioles and adjacent alveoli.
pathogenesis: Infection spreads from smaller airways into surrounding parenchyma. Host factors and the responsible organism influence whether foci remain patchy or become confluent.
gross: Multiple patchy areas of consolidation
Foci may be bilateral and more prominent in dependent regions
microscopy: Neutrophils within bronchioles
Suppurative exudate in adjacent alveoli
Patchy involvement with intervening better-preserved lung
clinical: Common in vulnerable hospitalized or debilitated patients
Severe disease may cause sepsis or respiratory failure
examTips: Bronchiolocentric distribution is more useful than trying to identify one specific organism from the pattern.

differentials.name: Lobar pneumonia
differentials.distinction: Produces a more confluent lobar consolidation.

stains: Gram stain may help demonstrate bacteria

name: Lung adenocarcinoma
definition: A malignant pulmonary epithelial tumour with glandular differentiation or mucin production.
pathogenesis: Genomic alterations drive clonal epithelial proliferation. Invasive growth can occur in acinar, papillary, lepidic, micropapillary or solid patterns, often in combination.
gross: Often a peripheral lung mass
Pleural puckering or a firm fibrotic centre may be present
microscopy: Malignant gland formation or intracellular mucin
Variable architectural patterns within the same tumour
Invasive tumour may be accompanied by desmoplastic stroma
clinical: Occurs in smokers and nonsmokers
Stage and molecular findings have important clinical implications
examTips: A lepidic component is growth along existing alveolar walls; invasion requires separate assessment.

differentials.name: Metastatic adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Immunophenotype and clinical imaging are needed to assess the primary site.

stains: TTF-1 and Napsin A support many pulmonary adenocarcinomas
Mucin stains can demonstrate glandular differentiation

name: Squamous cell carcinoma of lung
definition: A malignant lung epithelial tumour with squamous differentiation.
pathogenesis: Smoking-associated injury is an important risk factor. Accumulating genetic alterations can progress through dysplasia to invasive carcinoma.
gross: A central or peripheral solid mass
Central tumours may cavitate
microscopy: Keratinization in differentiated tumours
Intercellular bridges may be visible
Poorly differentiated tumours require ancillary assessment
clinical: May cause hemoptysis or obstructive pneumonia
Some tumours are associated with humoral hypercalcemia
examTips: Keratin pearls are helpful when present but are not required in every tumour.

differentials.name: Lung adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Shows glandular or mucinous differentiation rather than convincing squamous morphology.

stains: p40 supports squamous differentiation
CK5/6 is supportive in a suitable panel

Squamous cell carcinoma of lung gross pathology

name: Small cell lung carcinoma
definition: A high-grade pulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma composed of small cells with scant cytoplasm.
pathogenesis: Smoking-related molecular injury commonly disrupts tumour-suppressor pathways. Rapid proliferation and early dissemination account for its aggressive behavior.
gross: Often a central hilar mass
Nodal involvement and necrosis may be extensive
microscopy: Small cells with scant cytoplasm and finely granular chromatin
Nuclear molding and crush artifact
High mitotic activity and extensive necrosis
clinical: Can produce paraneoplastic endocrine or neurologic syndromes
Often disseminated at presentation
examTips: Crush artifact can make a biopsy difficult; do not confuse damaged lymphocytes with tumour without assessing viable areas.

differentials.name: Lymphoma
differentials.distinction: Requires correlation with cell morphology and epithelial versus hematolymphoid markers.

stains: Synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1 support neuroendocrine differentiation
Keratin supports carcinoma; Ki-67 is typically high
imageQueries: Small cell lung carcinoma gross pathology

name: Malignant mesothelioma
definition: An invasive malignant tumour arising from mesothelial surfaces, most often the pleura.
pathogenesis: Asbestos exposure is a major risk factor for pleural disease. Molecular alterations in mesothelial cells permit invasive epithelioid, sarcomatoid or biphasic growth.
gross: Diffuse pleural thickening may encase the lung
Pleural effusion is common
microscopy: Epithelioid tubules or papillary structures in some tumours
Sarcomatoid tumours show malignant spindle cells
Demonstrated invasion is important when assessing a mesothelial proliferation
clinical: Often presents with dyspnea or chest pain
A long interval may separate asbestos exposure from disease
examTips: No single positive mesothelial stain establishes malignancy.

differentials.name: Metastatic adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Use a balanced mesothelial and carcinoma immunohistochemical panel with clinical correlation.

stains: Calretinin, WT1 and D2-40 can support mesothelial differentiation
BAP1 loss or other validated ancillary findings may support malignancy

name: Silicosis
definition: A fibrosing pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of respirable crystalline silica.
pathogenesis: Macrophage activation and injury stimulate persistent inflammatory and fibrogenic responses. Repeated exposure can generate nodular fibrosis and, in advanced disease, conglomerate scarring.
gross: Firm pale nodules, often upper-lobe predominant
Advanced nodules may coalesce into large fibrotic masses
microscopy: Circumscribed nodules of whorled hyalinized collagen
Dust-laden macrophages at the periphery
Birefringent mineral particles may be seen with polarized light
clinical: Increases susceptibility to tuberculosis
Occupational exposure history is essential
examTips: A silicotic nodule is collagenous; do not mistake it for a necrotizing granuloma solely on a low-power view.

differentials.name: Tuberculosis
differentials.distinction: Caseating granulomas and microbiologic evidence support infection; both diseases may coexist.

stains: Polarized light helps reveal mineral particles
Acid-fast stains are used if tuberculosis is suspected

references.title: University of Utah WebPath: silicotic nodule

name: Asbestosis
definition: Diffuse interstitial pulmonary fibrosis caused by substantial inhaled asbestos exposure.
pathogenesis: Deposited fibres activate macrophages and stimulate fibrotic remodeling. Fibrosis often begins around respiratory bronchioles and progresses through the interstitium.
gross: Lower-lobe and subpleural fibrosis is typical
Pleural plaques may coexist but are not themselves proof of parenchymal asbestosis
microscopy: Interstitial fibrosis
Ferruginous bodies may contain a coated asbestos fibre
Advanced disease can show architectural distortion and honeycomb change
clinical: Can cause progressive restrictive respiratory impairment
Asbestos exposure also increases risks of lung carcinoma and mesothelioma
examTips: Pleural plaques mark exposure; diagnosis of asbestosis requires compatible parenchymal fibrosis.

differentials.name: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
differentials.distinction: Can resemble advanced disease, so fibre evidence and exposure assessment matter.

stains: Perls Prussian blue highlights iron coating on ferruginous bodies

name: Apoptosis
definition: Regulated cell death in which a cell fragments into membrane-bound bodies that are cleared by phagocytes.
pathogenesis: Intrinsic mitochondrial or extrinsic death-receptor signals activate caspases. Rapid removal of cell fragments usually limits inflammation.
gross: Usually no distinctive gross lesion in a small apoptotic focus
Macroscopic changes reflect the underlying process
microscopy: Cell shrinkage and dense eosinophilic cytoplasm
Condensed or fragmented chromatin
Discrete apoptotic bodies among viable cells
clinical: Occurs in normal tissue turnover as well as injury
Increased apoptosis may be seen in viral or drug-related injury
examTips: Apoptosis may be physiologic; necrosis is a different morphological pattern of cell death.

differentials.name: Necrosis
differentials.distinction: More often affects contiguous cells with membrane breakdown and an inflammatory response.

name: Granulation tissue
definition: New vascular connective tissue that participates in repair after tissue injury.
pathogenesis: Angiogenesis restores a vascular supply while fibroblasts migrate into the damaged area. Extracellular matrix accumulates and later remodels into less cellular scar.
gross: Soft red granular tissue in a healing wound
Tissue can bleed easily because of its abundant vessels
microscopy: Numerous thin-walled newly formed vessels
Plump fibroblasts in loose matrix
Mixed inflammatory cells, changing with time and cause
clinical: Seen in healing wounds and ulcer bases
Persistent injury can prevent maturation into scar
examTips: Granulation tissue is not a granuloma: the former is reparative and vessel-rich.

differentials.name: Granuloma
differentials.distinction: An organized collection of epithelioid histiocytes rather than a reparative fibrovascular proliferation.

name: Tuberculosis
definition: Infection by organisms of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex that can cause necrotizing granulomatous inflammation.
pathogenesis: Cell-mediated immunity recruits and activates macrophages around persistent organisms. Tissue destruction can produce caseation, cavitation or dissemination.
gross: Caseous nodules or lymph nodes
Pulmonary disease may cavitate; miliary disease produces tiny disseminated nodules
microscopy: Necrotizing epithelioid granulomas are characteristic but not universal
Langhans-type giant cells may occur
Acid-fast bacilli can be sparse or absent in a section
clinical: Clinical presentation depends on the organ involved
Immunosuppression can alter the usual granulomatous response
examTips: Negative tissue acid-fast stains do not exclude tuberculosis; microbiology and molecular studies may be needed.

differentials.name: Fungal infection
differentials.distinction: Can also produce necrotizing granulomas; morphology, stains and microbiology distinguish causes.

stains: Ziehl–Neelsen or auramine stains for acid-fast organisms
GMS or PAS for fungal differentials

name: Sarcoidosis
definition: A systemic granulomatous disorder diagnosed after excluding other causes of a compatible pattern.
pathogenesis: An incompletely understood immune response produces granulomas in susceptible individuals. The distribution and burden of inflammation determine organ dysfunction and eventual fibrosis.
gross: Enlarged hilar or other lymph nodes
Lung or other organs may contain pale nodules
microscopy: Well-formed epithelioid granulomas, usually non-necrotizing
Relatively sparse surrounding lymphocytes can create a naked appearance
Giant-cell inclusions may occur but are not specific
clinical: May involve lung, lymph nodes, skin or other organs
Clinical and imaging correlation is essential
examTips: Non-necrotizing granulomas alone do not prove sarcoidosis.

differentials.name: Mycobacterial or fungal infection
differentials.distinction: Must be considered and excluded using context and appropriate investigations.

stains: Acid-fast and fungal stains help investigate infectious mimics

name: Thrombosis
definition: Formation of a solid platelet–fibrin or blood-cell mass within the circulation during life.
pathogenesis: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability comprise Virchow's triad. Their relative contributions differ in arterial and venous thrombosis.
gross: A thrombus may be attached to the vessel wall
Older thrombi may organize and become incorporated into the wall
microscopy: Alternating platelet–fibrin and red-cell layers can form lines of Zahn
Organization brings fibroblasts and capillaries into the clot
Recanalization can create new channels
clinical: May obstruct blood flow or embolize
The anatomic setting determines the threatened tissue
examTips: Lines of Zahn support formation in flowing blood; their absence does not exclude an antemortem thrombus.

differentials.name: Postmortem clot
differentials.distinction: Usually lacks firm wall attachment and organized laminated platelet–fibrin structure.

name: Pulmonary thromboembolism
definition: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombi that usually originate in systemic deep veins.
pathogenesis: A venous thrombus detaches and travels through the right heart to the pulmonary circulation. The physiological effect depends on clot burden and cardiopulmonary reserve.
gross: A large embolus may straddle the main pulmonary arterial bifurcation
Peripheral infarcts, when present, are often hemorrhagic and wedge-shaped
microscopy: Intravascular fibrin, platelets and red cells
An older embolus may organize and recanalize
Hemorrhagic coagulative necrosis can occur in a peripheral infarct
clinical: May cause sudden dyspnea, chest pain or collapse
Many emboli do not produce a pulmonary infarct
examTips: Do not equate every pulmonary embolus with an infarct; the lung has a dual blood supply.

differentials.name: In situ pulmonary thrombosis
differentials.distinction: Forms locally in a pulmonary vessel rather than arriving as an embolus.

name: Dystrophic calcification
definition: Calcium-salt deposition in damaged or dead tissue despite a normal systemic calcium level.
pathogenesis: Injured membranes and local biochemical conditions favour calcium nucleation. Deposits can persist and enlarge after the original injury.
gross: Firm gritty white foci
Common in old scars, atheroma or damaged valves
microscopy: Basophilic granular or clumped mineral
Deposits occur in a damaged tissue background
Concentric lamination may be present in some settings
clinical: Can contribute to valve dysfunction
Calcification alone does not establish a particular etiology
examTips: Contrast local damaged-tissue deposition with metastatic calcification in otherwise viable tissue.

differentials.name: Metastatic calcification
differentials.distinction: Associated with disturbed calcium or phosphate metabolism and may involve otherwise normal tissues.

stains: Von Kossa highlights phosphate-containing mineral deposits

name: Squamous metaplasia
definition: Replacement of one differentiated epithelial type by squamous epithelium in response to altered conditions.
pathogenesis: Chronic irritation can redirect epithelial differentiation through changes in progenitor-cell programs. Continued injury can coexist with or precede dysplasia, but metaplasia is not itself cancer.
gross: Often no specific gross lesion
A chronically irritated surface may appear thickened
microscopy: Squamous epithelium at a site normally lined by another epithelial type
Maturation may be orderly
Atypia and invasion require separate assessment
clinical: May occur in irritated airways or other epithelial sites
The stimulus and organ context affect significance
examTips: Metaplasia describes cell-type change; dysplasia describes disordered growth and atypia.

differentials.name: Squamous dysplasia
differentials.distinction: Shows architectural disorder and cytologic atypia rather than simply a new mature epithelial type.

name: Epithelial dysplasia
definition: Disordered epithelial growth with architectural disturbance and cytologic atypia.
pathogenesis: Accumulated molecular damage can disturb proliferation, maturation and polarity. Some lesions progress toward invasive cancer, but the risk depends on site, grade and clinical setting.
gross: May form a visible mucosal lesion or be subtle
Gross appearance does not reliably grade dysplasia
microscopy: Loss of orderly maturation and polarity
Nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia and increased mitotic activity
An intact basement-membrane boundary separates in-situ change from stromal invasion
clinical: Used to assess precursor lesions at many epithelial sites
Diagnostic criteria and grading systems are organ-specific
examTips: Do not infer invasion from severe nuclear atypia alone.

differentials.name: Reactive atypia
differentials.distinction: Can accompany inflammation or repair; overall maturation, distribution and context help distinguish it.

references.title: National Cancer Institute: hyperplasia and dysplasia

name: Lipoma
definition: A benign neoplasm composed of mature adipose tissue.
pathogenesis: A clonal adipocytic proliferation forms a localized mass. Its clinical importance depends mainly on location, size and exclusion of atypical lipomatous tumours in appropriate settings.
gross: A soft yellow lobulated mass
Usually well circumscribed in superficial sites
microscopy: Mature adipocytes with relatively uniform nuclei
Thin delicate fibrous septa
No convincing atypical stromal cells in an ordinary lipoma
clinical: Commonly a slowly growing painless superficial mass
Deep or unusually large lesions need careful assessment
examTips: Mature fat does not automatically mean lipoma; evaluate the septa and any atypical cells.

differentials.name: Atypical lipomatous tumour
differentials.distinction: May contain atypical stromal cells and has characteristic MDM2 amplification in the correct setting.

name: Foreign-body granuloma
definition: A granulomatous reaction around material that macrophages cannot readily remove.
pathogenesis: Persistent material recruits macrophages and promotes multinucleated giant-cell formation. The reaction may coexist with fibrosis and a variable inflammatory infiltrate.
gross: A localized nodule may surround suture or other material
Gross appearance depends on the retained substance
microscopy: Histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells around foreign material
Material can be refractile or polarizable
Fibrosis and mixed inflammation may develop
clinical: Can occur after surgery, trauma or injected material
Some substances are difficult to see in routine sections
examTips: Search for material within and around giant cells; a foreign-body reaction does not exclude concurrent infection.

differentials.name: Infectious granuloma
differentials.distinction: Organisms or microbiologic evidence support an infectious cause.

stains: Polarized light can reveal some foreign materials
Organism stains are selected when infection is suspected

references.title: Libre Pathology: granuloma and foreign-body reactions

name: Barrett esophagus
definition: Replacement of distal esophageal squamous mucosa by metaplastic columnar mucosa; diagnostic criteria for intestinal metaplasia vary by guideline.
pathogenesis: Chronic gastroesophageal reflux can promote columnar metaplasia. In a subset, progressive molecular alterations lead to dysplasia and adenocarcinoma.
gross: Salmon-coloured mucosa can extend proximally from the gastroesophageal junction
Endoscopic landmarks and sampling determine interpretation
microscopy: Columnar epithelium in esophageal biopsies
Goblet cells establish intestinal metaplasia when present
Dysplasia is assessed separately from metaplasia
clinical: Associated with chronic reflux
Increases risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma, but most affected patients do not develop cancer
examTips: Goblet cells must be distinguished from mimics, and the biopsy location must be known.

differentials.name: Gastric cardia intestinal metaplasia
differentials.distinction: Can look identical microscopically; endoscopic localization is essential.

stains: Alcian blue can highlight acid mucin, interpreted with morphology

name: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
definition: An invasive malignant epithelial tumour with squamous differentiation arising in the esophagus.
pathogenesis: Tobacco, alcohol and other regional risk factors can contribute to epithelial damage. Dysplasia may progress to invasion through the mucosa into deeper tissues.
gross: An ulcerated, fungating or infiltrative esophageal lesion
Circumferential infiltration can narrow the lumen
microscopy: Invasive nests or cords of atypical squamous cells
Keratinization or intercellular bridges in differentiated areas
Desmoplastic stroma around invasive tumour
clinical: Progressive dysphagia is a common presentation
Local invasion and nodal spread affect stage
examTips: Assess invasion and extent; a superficial biopsy may not reveal the deepest disease.

differentials.name: Esophageal adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Shows glandular differentiation and often arises in a Barrett-associated setting.

stains: p40 or CK5/6 can support squamous differentiation in difficult cases
imageQueries: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma gross pathology

references.title: Libre Pathology: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma

name: Chronic gastritis
definition: Persistent gastric mucosal inflammation, sometimes accompanied by gland loss and intestinal metaplasia.
pathogenesis: Helicobacter pylori infection and autoimmune injury are major causes with different distributions. Ongoing inflammation can damage glands and alter epithelial differentiation.
gross: Mucosa may be unremarkable, erythematous or atrophic
Gross appearance alone cannot determine the cause
microscopy: Lymphocytes and plasma cells in the lamina propria
Neutrophils indicate activity
Glandular atrophy or intestinal metaplasia may accompany chronic injury
clinical: Can be associated with dyspepsia or be asymptomatic
Etiology determines risks such as ulcer disease, nutrient deficiency or neoplasia
examTips: Describe activity, atrophy and metaplasia separately rather than treating all chronic gastritis as one pattern.

differentials.name: Reactive gastropathy
differentials.distinction: Typically has foveolar hyperplasia and smooth-muscle changes with relatively little inflammation.

stains: H. pylori immunostain or special stains can help identify organisms

name: Peptic ulcer disease
definition: Mucosal ulceration in an acid-exposed region, usually the stomach or proximal duodenum.
pathogenesis: Acid–peptic injury exceeds mucosal defenses, commonly in association with H. pylori or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Repeated injury and repair create a chronic ulcer base.
gross: A sharply demarcated punched-out ulcer
Mucosal folds may radiate toward a benign-appearing ulcer margin
microscopy: Surface necrotic debris and inflammatory exudate
Underlying granulation tissue
Fibrous scar in a chronic ulcer base
clinical: Can cause pain, bleeding or perforation
A gastric ulcer requires assessment for underlying malignancy
examTips: A clean gross contour does not exclude gastric carcinoma; biopsy interpretation and adequate sampling matter.

differentials.name: Ulcerated carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Malignant glands or cells infiltrate the wall and may be missed by shallow sampling.

stains: H. pylori stains are selected when evaluating the background mucosa

name: Gastric adenocarcinoma
definition: A malignant gastric epithelial tumour with glandular or poorly cohesive differentiation.
pathogenesis: Chronic inflammatory and metaplastic pathways contribute to some tumours, while others have different molecular mechanisms. Invasive growth patterns range from gland-forming masses to diffuse wall infiltration.
gross: An ulcerated or fungating mass may be present
Diffuse infiltration can produce a rigid thickened linitis plastica stomach
microscopy: Irregular malignant glands in gland-forming tumours
Poorly cohesive or signet-ring cells in other tumours
Stromal invasion, desmoplasia and variable mucin
clinical: May present with weight loss, anemia or obstruction
Stage and biomarker assessment influence clinical management
examTips: A signet-ring cell is a morphological description; confirm epithelial malignancy and consider the clinical differential.

differentials.name: Reactive gastric glands
differentials.distinction: May be atypical near ulcers but lack convincing destructive invasion.

stains: Cytokeratins support epithelial differentiation
Mucin stains help demonstrate intracellular mucin

name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour
definition: A mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal tract associated with interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursors.
pathogenesis: Activating KIT or PDGFRA pathway alterations drive many cases, although molecularly distinct groups exist. Risk of aggressive behavior depends on site, size, mitotic activity and rupture status.
gross: A well-circumscribed mural or outward-growing mass
Large lesions can show hemorrhage, necrosis or mucosal ulceration
microscopy: Spindle cells, epithelioid cells or a mixture
Variable cellularity and stromal features
Mitotic activity must be assessed in the appropriate area
clinical: Often arises in stomach or small bowel
Can present with bleeding or mass effects
examTips: Do not label every GIST benign or malignant from bland appearance alone; use validated risk assessment.

differentials.name: Leiomyoma
differentials.distinction: Typically expresses smooth-muscle markers and lacks the usual KIT/DOG1 pattern.

stains: DOG1 and KIT support GIST in the appropriate morphology
A panel helps exclude smooth-muscle and neural mimics

name: Celiac disease
definition: An immune-mediated small-intestinal disorder triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible individuals.
pathogenesis: Gluten-associated immune responses injure mucosal epithelium in susceptible HLA backgrounds. The resulting inflammation alters the balance between villous maturation and crypt proliferation.
gross: Mucosal folds can be reduced or scalloped
A biopsy diagnosis cannot be made from gross appearance alone
microscopy: Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
Crypt hyperplasia
Villous blunting or atrophy in established disease
clinical: May cause malabsorption, anemia or extraintestinal manifestations
Serology, dietary history and biopsy orientation affect interpretation
examTips: Villous atrophy is not specific for celiac disease; exclude important mimics.

differentials.name: Giardiasis or drug-related enteropathy
differentials.distinction: May produce similar mucosal injury; clinical context and targeted investigations distinguish them.

stains: CD3 can assist assessment of intraepithelial T lymphocytes, but morphology and context remain essential

name: Crohn disease
definition: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any gastrointestinal segment and often involves the full bowel wall.
pathogenesis: An inappropriate immune response to intestinal contents develops in a susceptible host. Recurrent transmural inflammation can lead to fibrosis, strictures, fistulas and abscesses.
gross: Discontinuous skip lesions
Deep fissures, cobblestoning and creeping mesenteric fat may occur
microscopy: Patchy chronic active inflammation
Transmural lymphoid aggregates in resections
Non-necrotizing granulomas can support the diagnosis but are often absent
clinical: May cause abdominal pain, diarrhea or obstructive symptoms
Perianal or penetrating disease can occur
examTips: A mucosal biopsy cannot fully assess transmural inflammation; absence of granulomas does not exclude Crohn disease.

differentials.name: Ulcerative colitis
differentials.distinction: Usually has continuous mucosal disease beginning in the rectum rather than a classic transmural skip pattern.

stains: Organism stains may be needed when infection is a plausible mimic

name: Ulcerative colitis
definition: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease primarily involving the colorectal mucosa in a continuous distribution.
pathogenesis: An abnormal immune response produces recurrent mucosal injury. Longstanding inflammation can alter crypt architecture and increase colorectal neoplasia risk.
gross: Diffuse continuous mucosal inflammation, classically extending proximally from the rectum
Friability, superficial ulcers and inflammatory pseudopolyps can occur
microscopy: Crypt architectural distortion and basal plasmacytosis
Neutrophilic cryptitis and crypt abscesses during activity
Inflammation predominantly in mucosa outside severe or complicated disease
clinical: Typically causes bloody diarrhea and urgency
Disease duration and extent affect surveillance considerations
examTips: Treatment can alter distribution, so interpret patchiness with clinical history rather than one isolated rule.

differentials.name: Crohn disease
differentials.distinction: More often has transmural complications, skip lesions or well-formed non-crypt-injury granulomas.

stains: CMV immunostain may be appropriate in selected severe or refractory cases

name: Acute appendicitis
definition: Acute inflammation of the appendix, diagnosed histologically by appropriate mural neutrophilic inflammation.
pathogenesis: Luminal obstruction can contribute to increased pressure, impaired drainage and ischemic injury. Bacterial proliferation and wall inflammation may progress to suppuration, gangrene or perforation.
gross: A swollen congested appendix
Fibrinopurulent serosal exudate may cover advanced lesions
microscopy: Neutrophils infiltrating the muscularis propria
Mucosal ulceration and suppurative inflammation
Transmural necrosis in advanced disease
clinical: Usually presents with an acute abdominal syndrome
Perforation can cause peritonitis or an abscess
examTips: Neutrophils confined to the lumen do not automatically establish acute mural appendicitis.

differentials.name: Periappendicitis
differentials.distinction: Predominantly serosal inflammation can be secondary to a nearby inflammatory process.

name: Colorectal adenoma
definition: A dysplastic epithelial precursor lesion of the colon or rectum with conventional adenomatous differentiation.
pathogenesis: Clonal epithelial alterations generate dysplastic glands. Additional molecular changes can promote progression toward invasive carcinoma, although many adenomas never progress.
gross: A pedunculated or sessile mucosal polyp
Larger lesions may have a villous surface
microscopy: Crowded dysplastic glands with elongated hyperchromatic nuclei
Reduced surface maturation
Tubular, villous or mixed architecture
clinical: Often detected during screening
Size, number and pathological features influence follow-up
examTips: High-grade dysplasia remains noninvasive unless there is convincing invasion beyond the relevant mucosal boundary.

differentials.name: Hyperplastic polyp
differentials.distinction: Typically has serration without conventional cytologic dysplasia.

name: Colorectal adenocarcinoma
definition: An invasive malignant epithelial tumour of the large bowel, usually forming glands.
pathogenesis: Conventional adenoma–carcinoma and serrated pathways account for major subsets. Tumour progression allows stromal invasion and potential nodal or distant spread.
gross: A right-sided tumour may be polypoid or ulcerated
An annular constricting lesion can narrow the left-sided bowel
microscopy: Infiltrative malignant glands in desmoplastic stroma
Luminal dirty necrosis is common
Mucinous or other variant patterns may occur
clinical: Can cause bleeding, anemia or altered bowel habit
Depth of invasion, nodes and metastases determine stage
examTips: Distinguish invasive carcinoma from displaced glands in a polyp using the overall architecture and stromal response.

differentials.name: Colorectal adenoma
differentials.distinction: Dysplasia alone does not show destructive submucosal invasion.

stains: Mismatch-repair protein immunohistochemistry is important for appropriate tumour assessment
CDX2 and SATB2 may support colorectal differentiation in a panel

name: Hepatic steatosis
definition: Excess lipid accumulation within hepatocytes, most often as macrovesicular fat.
pathogenesis: Metabolic dysfunction, alcohol and other insults can disturb hepatic lipid handling. Steatosis can occur without steatohepatitis, so inflammation and hepatocyte injury must be evaluated separately.
gross: An enlarged yellow greasy liver may occur
The degree of gross change varies with the burden of fat
microscopy: Clear lipid vacuoles within hepatocytes after routine processing
Large droplets can displace the nucleus
Lobular distribution and accompanying injury vary
clinical: Often accompanies metabolic risk factors or alcohol exposure
Some patients progress to steatohepatitis and fibrosis
examTips: Fat alone is not enough to diagnose steatohepatitis.

differentials.name: Hepatocyte ballooning
differentials.distinction: Represents a form of cell injury rather than simply a large sharply outlined lipid droplet.

stains: Oil Red O can demonstrate lipid in suitable frozen material

name: Alcohol-associated hepatitis
definition: A pattern of hepatocellular injury associated with alcohol exposure and characterized by steatohepatitis in a suitable clinical setting.
pathogenesis: Alcohol-related metabolic and inflammatory injury damages hepatocytes. Repeated injury can produce pericellular fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis.
gross: The liver may be enlarged, yellow and firm
Advanced disease can have cirrhotic nodularity
microscopy: Steatosis with hepatocyte ballooning
Neutrophils may cluster around injured hepatocytes
Mallory–Denk bodies and pericellular fibrosis can occur
clinical: Clinical severity varies widely
Histology overlaps with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis
examTips: Mallory–Denk bodies are not specific for alcohol-related disease.

differentials.name: Metabolic steatohepatitis
differentials.distinction: May look similar; exposure history and metabolic context are essential.

stains: Trichrome highlights fibrosis

name: Chronic viral hepatitis
definition: Persistent virus-associated hepatic inflammation that can cause progressive fibrosis.
pathogenesis: An immune response against infected hepatocytes produces ongoing injury. The degree and distribution of inflammation and fibrosis differ by virus, host response and disease phase.
gross: Gross appearances may be subtle before advanced fibrosis
Progressive disease can produce cirrhotic nodularity
microscopy: Portal lymphocytic inflammation
Interface activity and lobular hepatocyte injury may occur
Fibrosis can bridge portal tracts and progress to cirrhosis
clinical: Can be clinically silent or associated with chronic liver dysfunction
Etiologic testing is required to establish the virus
examTips: Grade describes inflammatory activity; stage describes fibrosis extent.

differentials.name: Autoimmune hepatitis
differentials.distinction: May also show interface hepatitis; serology, immunoglobulins and the overall pattern are needed.

stains: Selected viral immunostains may be informative in context
Trichrome helps assess fibrosis

name: Cirrhosis
definition: Diffuse hepatic architectural distortion caused by bridging fibrosis and regenerative nodules.
pathogenesis: Chronic injury activates fibrogenic pathways while surviving hepatocytes regenerate. Fibrous septa and abnormal vascular relationships impair perfusion and liver function.
gross: A nodular liver surface
The organ may be enlarged or shrunken depending on cause and stage
microscopy: Regenerative hepatocyte nodules
Fibrous septa bridging vascular or portal structures
Loss of normal lobular architecture
clinical: Can produce portal hypertension and hepatic dysfunction
Increases risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in many settings
examTips: Cirrhosis is an architectural endpoint; assess clues to the underlying cause separately.

differentials.name: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia
differentials.distinction: Has regenerative nodularity without the diffuse bridging fibrosis of cirrhosis.

stains: Trichrome highlights fibrous septa
Reticulin helps assess architecture

name: Hepatocellular carcinoma
definition: A malignant epithelial tumour showing hepatocellular differentiation.
pathogenesis: Chronic liver disease and specific viral or metabolic factors can promote hepatocarcinogenesis. Molecular alterations enable abnormal trabecular, pseudoglandular or solid growth and vascular invasion.
gross: A single mass, multiple nodules or diffuse infiltration
Tumours may be yellow-green, hemorrhagic or necrotic
microscopy: Thickened hepatocyte-like trabeculae
Loss or disruption of the usual reticulin framework
Unpaired arteries, pseudoglands or bile production may be present
clinical: Often arises in a cirrhotic liver, but not invariably
Vascular invasion is an important adverse feature
examTips: A well-differentiated tumour can resemble benign liver; assess architecture and invasion rather than atypia alone.

differentials.name: Hepatocellular adenoma
differentials.distinction: Can resemble a well-differentiated carcinoma and requires integrated architectural, clinical and ancillary assessment.

stains: Arginase-1 and HepPar-1 support hepatocellular differentiation
Reticulin assesses the trabecular framework

name: Cholangiocarcinoma
definition: A malignant epithelial tumour arising from the biliary tract.
pathogenesis: Chronic biliary injury and other risk factors predispose to some cases, while others arise without a recognized precursor setting. Infiltrative glandular growth commonly produces a strong stromal response.
gross: A firm pale mass or infiltrative bile-duct lesion
Obstruction can dilate upstream ducts
microscopy: Irregular malignant glands
Dense desmoplastic stroma
Mucin production and perineural invasion may be present
clinical: Can cause cholestasis or a hepatic mass
Anatomic site determines the clinical presentation and staging approach
examTips: Morphology and CK7 positivity alone cannot exclude a metastatic pancreatobiliary-type adenocarcinoma.

differentials.name: Metastatic adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Requires clinical and imaging correlation with a suitable marker panel.

stains: CK7 and CK19 often support biliary differentiation in context

name: Chronic cholecystitis
definition: Chronic inflammation and fibromuscular remodeling of the gallbladder wall.
pathogenesis: Gallstones and repeated injury are common contributing factors. Ongoing inflammation and pressure can promote mural fibrosis and epithelial outpouchings.
gross: A thickened fibrotic gallbladder wall
Gallstones may be present
microscopy: Lymphocytes and plasma cells in the wall
Fibrosis and muscular hypertrophy
Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses may extend into the wall
clinical: Often associated with recurrent biliary symptoms
Gross and microscopic findings should be interpreted together
examTips: Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses are benign epithelial invaginations and can be mistaken for invasive glands.

differentials.name: Gallbladder adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Shows infiltrative atypical glands with convincing destructive growth or other malignant features.

name: Acute pancreatitis
definition: Acute pancreatic inflammation with variable acinar injury, edema, fat necrosis and hemorrhage.
pathogenesis: Premature activation of digestive enzymes initiates pancreatic injury. Inflammation and vascular damage can amplify necrosis locally and cause systemic complications.
gross: An edematous or hemorrhagic pancreas
Chalky foci of peripancreatic fat necrosis may be visible
microscopy: Acinar injury and necrosis
Acute inflammatory cells
Fat necrosis and hemorrhage in severe disease
clinical: Commonly associated with gallstones or alcohol, among other causes
Severity ranges from mild inflammation to extensive necrotizing disease
examTips: Saponification explains the chalky white fat-necrosis deposits.

differentials.name: Chronic pancreatitis
differentials.distinction: Has established fibrosis, acinar loss and ductal changes rather than solely an acute destructive process.

name: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
definition: An invasive gland-forming carcinoma of the pancreas with ductal differentiation.
pathogenesis: Accumulating molecular alterations can drive progression from ductal precursor lesions to invasive cancer. Tumour infiltration elicits prominent desmoplasia and often tracks along nerves.
gross: A hard ill-defined pale mass
A head-of-pancreas tumour can obstruct the bile duct
microscopy: Irregular angulated malignant glands
Dense desmoplastic stroma
Perineural and vascular invasion can be conspicuous
clinical: Can cause jaundice, weight loss or pain
An early lesion may be difficult to sample
examTips: Haphazard glands around large nerves or in abnormal locations help distinguish invasion from chronic pancreatitis.

differentials.name: Chronic pancreatitis
differentials.distinction: Fibrosis and distorted ducts can mimic cancer, but the overall architecture and cytology differ.

stains: A panel can support pancreatobiliary differentiation; no single stain replaces morphology

name: Minimal change disease
definition: A podocytopathy that typically produces nephrotic syndrome with little change on routine light microscopy.
pathogenesis: Podocyte dysfunction disrupts the filtration barrier. The resulting foot-process effacement is detected by electron microscopy rather than by a conspicuous proliferative lesion.
gross: No characteristic gross lesion
Kidneys may appear normal or enlarged
microscopy: Glomeruli are near normal by light microscopy
Immunofluorescence is usually negative or nonspecific
Diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy
clinical: An important cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome
Can also occur in adults and in secondary settings
examTips: A near-normal light-microscopic biopsy does not exclude important glomerular disease.

differentials.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
differentials.distinction: Shows segmental sclerosis in some glomeruli, which can be missed by limited sampling.

stains: Electron microscopy is central
Immunofluorescence helps exclude immune-complex disease

name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
definition: A pattern of segmental scarring affecting a subset of glomeruli, arising from several causes of podocyte injury.
pathogenesis: Primary, genetic and adaptive mechanisms can damage podocytes. Loss of podocyte integrity promotes protein leakage, capillary collapse and segmental matrix accumulation.
gross: No specific gross appearance early
Chronic disease may produce contracted scarred kidneys
microscopy: Segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis in some glomeruli
Adhesions to Bowman's capsule may occur
Foot-process effacement varies with the form and extent of injury
clinical: Often associated with proteinuria
The lesion is a pattern that requires etiologic classification
examTips: Focal means some glomeruli; segmental means only part of an affected glomerulus.

differentials.name: Minimal change disease
differentials.distinction: Lacks a definite sclerosing lesion, but limited sampling can obscure early focal disease.

stains: PAS and silver stains assess the sclerosing lesion
Electron microscopy evaluates podocyte injury

name: Membranous nephropathy
definition: An immune-mediated glomerular disease with subepithelial immune deposits and capillary-wall remodeling.
pathogenesis: Antibodies bind podocyte-associated antigens in primary disease or other targets in secondary settings. Complement-mediated injury and matrix deposition disrupt filtration and thicken capillary walls.
gross: No distinctive gross lesion in early disease
Longstanding damage can lead to chronic scarring
microscopy: Diffuse capillary-wall thickening may develop
Granular capillary-loop immune deposits on immunofluorescence
Subepithelial electron-dense deposits and basement-membrane spikes
clinical: Commonly produces nephrotic syndrome in adults
Primary and secondary causes require different investigations
examTips: Spikes represent new basement-membrane material between deposits, not the deposits themselves.

differentials.name: Diabetic glomerulosclerosis
differentials.distinction: Has different mesangial and vascular changes and lacks the usual granular subepithelial immune-deposit pattern.

stains: Silver stain highlights basement-membrane spikes
PLA2R staining is useful in suitable cases

name: IgA nephropathy
definition: A glomerular disease characterized by dominant or codominant mesangial IgA deposition.
pathogenesis: Abnormally glycosylated IgA1 and immune responses promote mesangial immune-complex accumulation. Mesangial activation and complement pathways cause variable glomerular injury.
gross: Usually no characteristic gross lesion
Chronic disease can result in scarring
microscopy: Mesangial hypercellularity can be present
Mesangial dominant or codominant IgA on immunofluorescence
Mesangial electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy
clinical: Often presents with hematuria, sometimes close to a mucosal infection
The course ranges from indolent to progressive
examTips: Diagnosis relies on the immunofluorescence pattern in an appropriate clinical setting.

differentials.name: IgA vasculitis
differentials.distinction: Can have similar renal findings but is accompanied by a systemic small-vessel vasculitic syndrome.

stains: IgA and complement immunofluorescence
Electron microscopy helps characterize deposits

name: Infection-related glomerulonephritis
definition: Immune-mediated glomerular inflammation occurring during or after an infection.
pathogenesis: Microbial antigens and host immune responses lead to glomerular immune deposition and complement activation. Injury can be diffuse, exudative or crescentic depending on the setting.
gross: Kidneys may be enlarged and pale
Small cortical hemorrhages can occur
microscopy: Endocapillary hypercellularity with neutrophils in a typical exudative lesion
Granular immune deposits on immunofluorescence
Subepithelial hump-like deposits may be seen on electron microscopy
clinical: Can cause an acute nephritic presentation
The clinical context differs between poststreptococcal disease and infection-associated disease in adults
examTips: A hump-like deposit is a clue, not a standalone etiologic diagnosis.

differentials.name: C3 glomerulopathy
differentials.distinction: May overlap morphologically and requires integrated complement and follow-up assessment.

stains: Immunofluorescence for immunoglobulins and complement
Electron microscopy assesses deposit location

name: Diabetic nephropathy
definition: A pattern of glomerular, vascular and tubulointerstitial injury associated with diabetes mellitus.
pathogenesis: Chronic metabolic and hemodynamic stress thickens basement membranes and promotes extracellular matrix accumulation. Progressive glomerular and vascular injury can produce proteinuria and declining renal function.
gross: Kidneys can be enlarged early
Advanced disease may produce granular contracted kidneys
microscopy: Diffuse mesangial matrix expansion
Nodular glomerulosclerosis can form Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules
Glomerular basement-membrane thickening and arteriolar hyalinosis
clinical: Associated with albuminuria and chronic kidney disease
Atypical clinical features can suggest a concurrent renal disease
examTips: Not every renal lesion in a person with diabetes is diabetic nephropathy.

differentials.name: Amyloidosis
differentials.distinction: Can also produce nodular glomerular deposits but is Congo-red positive.

stains: PAS and silver stains assess mesangium and basement membranes
Congo red helps investigate amyloid when indicated

name: Acute tubular injury
definition: Acute damage to renal tubular epithelium, often with limited overt necrosis despite the traditional term acute tubular necrosis.
pathogenesis: Ischemia or nephrotoxins impair tubular cell integrity and transport. Tubular obstruction, epithelial detachment and altered intrarenal hemodynamics contribute to acute kidney injury.
gross: Kidneys may be swollen and pale
Gross changes may be subtle
microscopy: Tubular epithelial simplification and loss of brush borders
Luminal cellular debris or granular casts
Focal epithelial detachment and regenerative mitoses may occur
clinical: A common pathological correlate of acute kidney injury
The extent of microscopy may not parallel clinical severity
examTips: Use acute tubular injury when appropriate; widespread necrosis is not required.

differentials.name: Acute interstitial nephritis
differentials.distinction: More prominently targets the interstitium with inflammatory infiltration and tubulitis.

name: Chronic pyelonephritis
definition: Chronic tubulointerstitial scarring associated with recurrent infection, reflux or obstruction in the appropriate setting.
pathogenesis: Repeated injury destroys tubules and promotes interstitial fibrosis. Reflux or impaired drainage can produce an uneven distribution of chronic damage.
gross: Irregular asymmetric cortical scars
Calyceal blunting or dilation may accompany scars
microscopy: Tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis
Chronic inflammatory infiltrates
Dilated tubules with eosinophilic casts can create thyroidization
clinical: Can contribute to hypertension or chronic renal impairment
Anatomical and clinical correlation helps establish the cause
examTips: Thyroidization is not unique to pyelonephritis; it can occur in other chronic tubulointerstitial diseases.

differentials.name: Other chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis
differentials.distinction: Can share the microscopic pattern without the same infection or reflux setting.

name: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
definition: A malignant renal epithelial tumour with clear or eosinophilic cells and a characteristic delicate vascular network.
pathogenesis: VHL pathway disruption and related molecular events drive many tumours. Lipid and glycogen accumulation contributes to the clear cytoplasmic appearance in routine sections.
gross: A golden-yellow renal mass
Hemorrhage, necrosis or cystic change may occur
microscopy: Nests, sheets or alveolar groups of clear cells
Delicate branching capillary vasculature
Variable nuclear grade and areas of eosinophilic cytoplasm
clinical: May present with hematuria or be incidental
Renal vein invasion and metastatic spread are important features
examTips: The classic yellow colour and clear cells are helpful, but use the full architectural and immunophenotypic context.

differentials.name: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumour
differentials.distinction: Has a different architectural and immunophenotypic pattern and usually indolent behavior.

stains: PAX8 supports renal lineage
CAIX and other markers help classify the tumour
imageQueries: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma histopathology
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma gross pathology

references.title: Libre Pathology: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma

name: Wilms tumour
definition: A childhood renal embryonal tumour that can show blastemal, epithelial and stromal differentiation.
pathogenesis: Disordered renal developmental pathways allow persistence and proliferation of immature elements. Molecular and syndromic associations vary among patients.
gross: A large pale renal mass
Hemorrhage and necrosis can occur
microscopy: Variable combination of blastema, epithelial tubules and stroma
Some tumours are monophasic rather than fully triphasic
Anaplasia must be assessed separately
clinical: Usually presents in young children
An abdominal mass is a common presentation
examTips: Triphasic morphology is classic but not mandatory in every sampled section.

differentials.name: Neuroblastoma
differentials.distinction: Can also be a childhood small-round-cell tumour; location, neuropil and lineage markers help distinguish it.

stains: WT1 can support the diagnosis in an appropriate panel

name: Urothelial carcinoma
definition: A malignant epithelial tumour arising from the urothelial lining of the urinary tract.
pathogenesis: Carcinogenic exposures and molecular alterations produce papillary or flat precursor pathways. Invasion into deeper tissues changes stage and prognosis.
gross: Papillary fronds or an irregular infiltrative lesion
Some high-grade lesions are flat and grossly subtle
microscopy: Papillary fibrovascular cores in papillary tumours
Cytologic and architectural atypia graded in context
Invasive nests or single cells may enter lamina propria or muscle
clinical: Hematuria is a common presentation
The tumour can arise anywhere along the urothelial tract
examTips: Muscularis propria must be distinguished from muscularis mucosae when assessing invasion.

differentials.name: Reactive urothelial atypia
differentials.distinction: May accompany inflammation or instrumentation without the architectural and cytologic pattern of carcinoma.

stains: GATA3 and uroplakins can support urothelial differentiation in a panel

name: Iron-deficiency anemia
definition: Anemia caused by insufficient available iron for normal hemoglobin production.
pathogenesis: Iron loss, inadequate intake, increased requirements or impaired absorption deplete iron stores. Reduced hemoglobin synthesis eventually produces microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes.
gross: No characteristic gross tissue lesion
An underlying bleeding source must be sought when appropriate
microscopy: Microcytosis and increased central pallor on a blood film
Anisopoikilocytosis with pencil-shaped cells may occur
Marrow iron stores are reduced when appropriately assessed
clinical: Can cause fatigue and pallor
The cause of iron deficiency is as important as recognizing the blood-film pattern
examTips: Microcytosis is a pattern; use iron studies and clinical context to distinguish its causes.

differentials.name: Thalassemia trait
differentials.distinction: Can have marked microcytosis with a relatively preserved red-cell count and different iron studies.

stains: Perls Prussian blue can assess marrow iron when marrow examination is otherwise indicated

references.title: University of Utah WebPath: microcytic hypochromic blood film

name: Megaloblastic anemia
definition: Anemia with impaired DNA synthesis causing asynchronous maturation of nucleus and cytoplasm.
pathogenesis: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency and some drugs impair DNA synthesis in proliferating cells. Ineffective hematopoiesis produces abnormal precursors and may affect multiple cell lines.
gross: No specific gross lesion in the blood
The cause may involve gastric or intestinal disease rather than a primary marrow mass
microscopy: Macro-ovalocytes on a peripheral smear
Hypersegmented neutrophils
Large marrow precursors with immature nuclear chromatin relative to cytoplasmic maturation
clinical: Can produce anemia and other cytopenias
Neurologic features raise particular concern for vitamin B12 deficiency
examTips: Macrocytosis alone does not establish megaloblastic anemia; assess smear, biochemical findings and cause.

differentials.name: Nonmegaloblastic macrocytosis
differentials.distinction: Can accompany liver disease, alcohol exposure or reticulocytosis without the classic maturation abnormality.

references.title: University of Utah WebPath: megaloblastic blood film

name: Aplastic anemia
definition: Bone-marrow failure characterized by reduced hematopoiesis and peripheral cytopenias without a malignant marrow replacement.
pathogenesis: Immune-mediated injury is a common acquired mechanism, while toxins, drugs and inherited disorders are other considerations. Loss of stem and progenitor cells produces a fatty hypocellular marrow.
gross: Marrow is replaced predominantly by fat
There is no defining solid tumour mass
microscopy: Marked hypocellularity for age
Reduction of hematopoietic lineages
Residual small islands of hematopoiesis may remain
clinical: Can present with fatigue, infection or bleeding
Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of hypocellular marrow failure
examTips: A fatty marrow core must be interpreted for age, sampling and clinical context.

differentials.name: Hypocellular myelodysplastic neoplasm
differentials.distinction: May show dysplasia or clonal abnormalities rather than otherwise bland aplasia.

name: Sickle cell disease
definition: An inherited hemoglobin disorder in which hemoglobin S can polymerize and distort red cells.
pathogenesis: Deoxygenated hemoglobin S polymerizes under susceptible conditions. Repeated sickling causes hemolysis, endothelial injury and vaso-occlusion.
gross: Repeated splenic infarction can result in a small fibrotic spleen
Bone or other organs may show ischemic injury
microscopy: Sickled erythrocytes on blood films or in vessels
Polychromasia and other features of hemolysis may coexist
Organ sections can show congestion, infarction or chronic damage
clinical: Produces chronic hemolysis and episodic vaso-occlusive complications
Functional hyposplenism increases infection risk
examTips: A blood film can suggest sickling, but hemoglobin analysis establishes the hemoglobin pattern.

differentials.name: Thalassemia
differentials.distinction: Has impaired globin-chain production rather than hemoglobin S polymerization as the central mechanism.

name: Thalassemia
definition: A group of inherited disorders with reduced production of alpha- or beta-globin chains.
pathogenesis: Imbalanced globin synthesis damages developing erythrocytes and promotes ineffective erythropoiesis. Hemolysis and compensatory marrow expansion contribute to disease severity.
gross: Marrow expansion can alter bone architecture in severe disease
Splenomegaly and secondary iron loading may occur
microscopy: Microcytosis and hypochromia
Target cells and variable anisopoikilocytosis
Nucleated red cells may circulate in severe disease
clinical: Severity ranges from an asymptomatic trait to transfusion-dependent disease
Hemoglobin studies and genetic context distinguish subtypes
examTips: Target cells are useful clues but are not specific to thalassemia.

differentials.name: Iron-deficiency anemia
differentials.distinction: Usually has depleted iron stores and a different biochemical profile.

name: Hereditary spherocytosis
definition: An inherited red-cell membrane disorder causing spherical erythrocytes and predominantly extravascular hemolysis.
pathogenesis: Defects in membrane–cytoskeleton proteins reduce membrane surface area relative to cell volume. Poorly deformable spherocytes are removed by the spleen.
gross: Splenomegaly can occur
Chronic hemolysis may lead to pigment gallstones
microscopy: Small dense spherocytes lacking the usual central pallor
Polychromasia with reticulocytosis
Marrow erythroid hyperplasia may accompany hemolysis
clinical: Can cause anemia, jaundice and episodic worsening
Family history and confirmatory membrane testing are useful
examTips: Spherocytes also occur in immune hemolysis; they do not prove an inherited disorder.

differentials.name: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
differentials.distinction: Can also produce spherocytes, often with a positive direct antiglobulin test in the appropriate setting.

name: G6PD deficiency
definition: An inherited enzymatic disorder that makes red cells vulnerable to oxidant-induced hemolysis.
pathogenesis: Reduced NADPH generation limits protection against oxidative stress. Oxidant exposure can denature hemoglobin and damage the red-cell membrane.
gross: No characteristic gross lesion during a mild episode
Severe hemolysis can affect multiple organs
microscopy: Bite cells and blister cells may appear on a smear
Heinz bodies require a suitable supravital stain
Polychromasia may accompany recovery
clinical: Hemolysis can be episodic after infection or oxidant exposure
Testing during acute hemolysis can be misleading because the surviving population is enriched for younger cells
examTips: A routine H&E or standard blood-film stain does not reliably reveal Heinz bodies.

differentials.name: Other oxidant hemolysis
differentials.distinction: Can also produce Heinz bodies and bite cells without inherited G6PD deficiency.

stains: Supravital stains can demonstrate Heinz bodies

name: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
definition: Hemolysis caused by immune reactions directed against red cells.
pathogenesis: Antibodies and sometimes complement mark erythrocytes for destruction. The dominant mechanism varies between warm-antibody and cold-antibody forms.
gross: Splenomegaly may occur in some cases
No single gross finding establishes immune hemolysis
microscopy: Spherocytes may occur in warm-antibody disease
Polychromasia reflects marrow response
Red-cell agglutination can appear in cold-antibody settings
clinical: Can present with anemia and jaundice
The direct antiglobulin test is interpreted with evidence of hemolysis
examTips: A positive direct antiglobulin test alone does not prove active hemolysis.

differentials.name: Hereditary spherocytosis
differentials.distinction: Can share spherocytes but has a different mechanism and confirmatory testing.

references.title: NHLBI: hemolytic anemia and immune causes

name: Acute myeloid leukemia
definition: A clonal myeloid neoplasm with an acute leukemic presentation, classified using integrated morphology, immunophenotype and genetics.
pathogenesis: Acquired molecular alterations disrupt normal myeloid differentiation and proliferation. Leukemic cells replace effective marrow hematopoiesis and can infiltrate tissues.
gross: Marrow may be soft and hypercellular
Extramedullary myeloid masses can occur
microscopy: Blasts with variable myeloid differentiation
Auer rods may be present in some forms
Residual normal hematopoiesis is often reduced
clinical: Can cause cytopenias, infection or bleeding
Specific genetic categories have distinct diagnostic criteria
examTips: Do not apply a single blast threshold without considering genetically defined categories and the current classification.

differentials.name: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
differentials.distinction: Requires lineage distinction by flow cytometry and other ancillary findings.

stains: Myeloperoxidase supports myeloid differentiation
Flow cytometry is central to lineage assessment

name: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
definition: A precursor lymphoid neoplasm involving marrow and blood, of B- or T-cell lineage.
pathogenesis: Genetic alterations arrest lymphoid maturation and promote proliferation. Expanding lymphoblasts suppress normal marrow function and can involve extramedullary sites.
gross: Marrow is commonly hypercellular
Lymphadenopathy or an extramedullary mass may be present
microscopy: Relatively uniform immature lymphoid cells
Scant cytoplasm and fine chromatin in many cases
High proliferative activity
clinical: Often presents with marrow failure or tissue infiltration
Age and molecular subtype affect disease context
examTips: Morphology alone cannot reliably distinguish B-ALL, T-ALL and some myeloid leukemias.

differentials.name: Acute myeloid leukemia
differentials.distinction: Myeloid lineage markers or lineage-defining genetic findings support AML.

stains: TdT often marks precursor cells
Flow cytometry distinguishes B- and T-lineage differentiation

references.title: National Cancer Institute: acute lymphoblastic leukemia

name: Chronic myeloid leukemia
definition: A myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by BCR::ABL1 in the appropriate clinicopathological setting.
pathogenesis: The BCR::ABL1 fusion encodes an active tyrosine kinase; the classic Philadelphia chromosome arises from t(9;22). Clonal myeloid proliferation expands the granulocytic series and can progress to advanced disease.
gross: Splenomegaly can be marked
Marrow is commonly hypercellular
microscopy: Granulocytes at multiple maturation stages in blood
Basophilia is an important clue
Marrow granulocytic hyperplasia with often small hypolobated megakaryocytes
clinical: Can be detected through leukocytosis or splenic symptoms
Disease phase requires integrated evaluation
examTips: Confirm BCR::ABL1 rather than diagnosing CML from leukocytosis alone.

differentials.name: Leukemoid reaction
differentials.distinction: Reactive granulocytic expansion lacks the defining fusion and has a different clinical context.

name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma
definition: A mature clonal B-cell neoplasm designated by its pattern and degree of blood or tissue involvement.
pathogenesis: Clonal small B cells accumulate in blood, marrow and lymphoid tissues. The tissue counterpart forms proliferation centres containing larger activated cells.
gross: Lymph nodes can be diffusely enlarged
Splenomegaly may occur
microscopy: Small lymphocytes with condensed chromatin
Smudge cells are common on blood films but not specific
Tissue may contain pale proliferation centres
clinical: Often an indolent disease in older adults
