Autoimmune cytopenias and transformation can complicate the course
examTips: The characteristic phenotype must be interpreted with the clonal B-cell count and tissue findings.

differentials.name: Mantle cell lymphoma
differentials.distinction: Can share CD5 positivity but usually has a different cyclin D1/SOX11 and genetic profile.

stains: Flow cytometry typically demonstrates a characteristic CD5-positive B-cell phenotype
CD23 and other markers are interpreted as a panel

name: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma
definition: A B-cell-derived lymphoma with scattered characteristic neoplastic cells in a prominent reactive background.
pathogenesis: Molecular and immune-evasion changes permit survival of Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells. The surrounding inflammatory milieu often dominates the tissue appearance.
gross: Enlarged lymph nodes, sometimes in a contiguous distribution
Some subtypes produce a firm fibrotic cut surface
microscopy: Large atypical Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cells
A mixed reactive inflammatory background
Fibrous bands and lacunar-type cells can occur in nodular sclerosis
clinical: Often presents with lymphadenopathy
Systemic symptoms can occur
examTips: Reed–Sternberg-like cells occur in other conditions; diagnose with architecture, context and immunophenotype.

differentials.name: Reactive EBV-associated immunoblasts
differentials.distinction: Can resemble tumour cells but occur in a different overall architecture and phenotype.

stains: CD30 is commonly positive
CD15 and weak PAX5 are useful in an appropriate panel

name: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
definition: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with diffuse proliferation of large lymphoid cells.
pathogenesis: Diverse molecular alterations generate a heterogeneous family of large B-cell neoplasms. Disease can arise de novo or through transformation of a prior indolent lymphoma.
gross: A fleshy nodal or extranodal mass
Necrosis may occur in rapidly growing lesions
microscopy: Diffuse architectural effacement by large atypical lymphoid cells
Prominent nucleoli and brisk mitotic activity
Variable cell morphology and background
clinical: Often presents as a rapidly enlarging mass
Integrated classification requires immunophenotypic and genetic assessment
examTips: Do not diagnose a large-cell lymphoma from size alone; establish lineage and exclude mimics.

differentials.name: Metastatic carcinoma
differentials.distinction: May form cohesive groups and expresses epithelial rather than hematolymphoid markers.

stains: CD20 and PAX5 support B-cell lineage
A broader panel and selected genetic studies guide classification
imageQueries: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma blood smear

references.title: Libre Pathology: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

name: Follicular lymphoma
definition: A mature B-cell lymphoma with germinal-centre differentiation and often a follicular growth pattern.
pathogenesis: Dysregulated survival pathways, commonly involving BCL2 in classic forms, promote persistence of germinal-centre B cells. Additional changes influence grade, growth pattern and transformation risk.
gross: Enlarged lymph nodes
Extranodal sites may also be involved
microscopy: Crowded abnormal follicles with reduced polarization
Centrocytes and variable centroblasts
Mantle zones and tingible-body macrophages are often reduced
clinical: Often presents as an indolent nodal lymphoma
Transformation to an aggressive lymphoma can occur
examTips: Assess the entire architecture and phenotype; BCL2 expression has exceptions and is not a standalone diagnosis.

differentials.name: Reactive follicular hyperplasia
differentials.distinction: Typically retains polarization, mantle zones and numerous tingible-body macrophages.

stains: CD10 and BCL6 support germinal-centre differentiation
BCL2 is interpreted with the architecture and other findings

name: Burkitt lymphoma
definition: A highly proliferative mature B-cell lymphoma with characteristic morphology and MYC-associated biology.
pathogenesis: MYC dysregulation, classically through t(8;14) involving the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus or a light-chain variant, drives rapid cell cycling. Apoptosis and brisk proliferation create a characteristic cellular turnover pattern.
gross: A rapidly growing nodal or extranodal mass
Abdominal or jaw involvement can occur in different epidemiologic settings
microscopy: Monomorphic medium-sized lymphoid cells
Numerous mitoses and apoptotic bodies
Tingible-body macrophages can create a starry-sky pattern
clinical: Can cause rapidly progressive mass effects
Tumour burden may be high
examTips: Starry-sky morphology is not specific; integrate the phenotype and genetics.

differentials.name: Other high-grade B-cell lymphomas
differentials.distinction: Can overlap morphologically and require integrated classification.

stains: CD10 and BCL6 commonly support germinal-centre phenotype
Ki-67 is very high; MYC testing is interpreted in context

name: Plasma cell myeloma
definition: A clonal plasma-cell neoplasm diagnosed by integrated marrow, laboratory, imaging and clinical criteria.
pathogenesis: A plasma-cell clone expands within marrow and may produce a monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chain. Bone and organ injury result from both tumour burden and secreted products.
gross: Lytic skeletal lesions can occur
Marrow may contain focal or diffuse tumour deposits
microscopy: Clonal plasma cells with eccentric nuclei
Perinuclear clearing and coarse chromatin may be present
Atypical or plasmablastic forms can occur
clinical: Can produce anemia, renal injury, hypercalcemia or bone lesions
A monoclonal protein alone does not establish myeloma
examTips: Differentiate a clonal plasma-cell finding from a myeloma-defining clinical syndrome.

differentials.name: Reactive plasmacytosis
differentials.distinction: Usually has a polytypic light-chain pattern and an appropriate reactive setting.

stains: CD138 highlights plasma cells
Kappa/lambda studies assess light-chain restriction

name: Immune thrombocytopenia
definition: An immune-mediated thrombocytopenia diagnosed after excluding important alternative causes.
pathogenesis: Immune destruction of platelets and impaired platelet production contribute to low circulating counts. The marrow may retain or increase megakaryocytes, but that finding is not diagnostic by itself.
gross: Petechiae or other bleeding manifestations may occur
There is no defining gross marrow lesion
microscopy: Peripheral smear shows reduced platelets, sometimes with larger forms
Megakaryocytes may be preserved or increased in marrow
No specific histological feature confirms the diagnosis
clinical: Can present with mucocutaneous bleeding or an incidental low count
Other causes of thrombocytopenia must be excluded
examTips: Exclude pseudothrombocytopenia by reviewing the blood film and sampling context.

differentials.name: Marrow failure
differentials.distinction: Usually has additional abnormalities or reduced effective hematopoiesis rather than isolated immune platelet destruction.

name: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
definition: Systemic activation of coagulation with microvascular fibrin formation and consumption of platelets and clotting factors.
pathogenesis: A severe underlying illness activates widespread coagulation. Thrombosis, factor consumption and secondary fibrinolysis can produce simultaneous ischemia and bleeding.
gross: Petechial or larger hemorrhages may occur
Organs can show ischemic damage
microscopy: Fibrin thrombi in small vessels
Associated ischemic tissue injury
Hemorrhage can accompany consumption of hemostatic components
clinical: Occurs in settings such as severe infection, obstetric complications or malignancy
Diagnosis combines clinical context with serial coagulation and platelet findings
examTips: DIC is a secondary syndrome; identify the precipitating disorder.

differentials.name: Thrombotic microangiopathy
differentials.distinction: Can also cause microangiopathic hemolysis and platelet consumption but usually has a different coagulation profile.

name: Polycythemia vera
definition: A myeloproliferative neoplasm with increased red-cell production and characteristic integrated molecular and marrow findings.
pathogenesis: JAK2-associated signaling abnormalities drive clonal hematopoiesis in most cases. Expansion often affects multiple myeloid lineages, not only erythrocytes.
gross: Splenomegaly may occur
Marrow can be hypercellular
microscopy: Trilineage proliferation in an appropriate marrow specimen
Pleomorphic mature megakaryocytes
Increased erythroid and granulocytic elements
clinical: Can present with erythrocytosis or thrombotic complications
Secondary causes and relative erythrocytosis require exclusion
examTips: An elevated hemoglobin value alone does not establish polycythemia vera.

differentials.name: Secondary erythrocytosis
differentials.distinction: Usually has a physiological or pathological stimulus rather than the characteristic clonal marrow pattern.

name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
definition: Benign nodular proliferation of prostatic glands and stroma, usually centred in the transition-zone region.
pathogenesis: Age-related hormonal signaling supports stromal and glandular proliferation. Nodular enlargement can compress the urethra and impair urinary outflow.
gross: An enlarged nodular prostate
Nodules can be variably glandular, cystic or fibromuscular
microscopy: Proliferation of glands and fibromuscular stroma
Glands retain a basal-cell layer
Papillary infoldings and luminal corpora amylacea may occur
clinical: Can cause lower urinary tract symptoms
It is not considered a direct precursor of ordinary prostatic adenocarcinoma
examTips: Hyperplasia means increased cell number; the common term prostatic hypertrophy is imprecise.

differentials.name: Prostatic adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Shows infiltrative malignant glands with loss of the usual basal-cell layer.

stains: Basal-cell markers can help in selected difficult glandular lesions

name: Prostatic adenocarcinoma
definition: An invasive malignant gland-forming epithelial tumour of the prostate.
pathogenesis: Accumulated molecular alterations allow abnormal acinar growth and stromal invasion. Many ordinary acinar carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, although location is not absolute.
gross: A firm pale or gritty area may be subtle
Tumour can be multifocal and difficult to distinguish grossly
microscopy: Small infiltrative glands or more complex malignant patterns
Prominent nucleoli may be present
Loss of basal cells and perineural invasion can support the diagnosis
clinical: May be detected through screening or symptoms
Grade, stage and clinical factors guide risk assessment
examTips: Gleason grading assesses architectural patterns, not simply nuclear atypia.

differentials.name: Benign prostatic atrophy
differentials.distinction: Can form small crowded glands but lacks convincing malignant architecture and usually retains basal cells.

stains: p63 and high-molecular-weight keratin assess basal cells
AMACR is supportive but not independently diagnostic

name: Seminoma
definition: A malignant testicular germ-cell tumour composed of relatively uniform seminomatous cells.
pathogenesis: Most postpubertal cases are related to germ-cell neoplasia in situ. Tumour cells proliferate in sheets or lobules, often eliciting a lymphocytic response.
gross: A homogeneous pale tan or white testicular mass
Hemorrhage and necrosis are less prominent than in many nonseminomatous tumours
microscopy: Large cells with clear or pale cytoplasm
Central nuclei with prominent nucleoli
Fibrous septa and lymphocytes commonly separate tumour lobules
clinical: Usually presents as a testicular mass
Serum markers and staging are interpreted with the complete tumour composition
examTips: A raised AFP is not explained by pure seminoma and prompts assessment for another component or cause.

differentials.name: Embryonal carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Often has more pleomorphism, cohesive epithelial architecture and CD30 expression.

stains: OCT4 and CD117 commonly support seminoma
A panel distinguishes other germ-cell tumours

name: Embryonal carcinoma
definition: A malignant primitive germ-cell tumour that often occurs as a component of mixed germ-cell tumours.
pathogenesis: Immature germ cells acquire embryonal-type differentiation and invasive growth. The tumour can adopt solid, glandular or papillary patterns and commonly shows necrosis.
gross: A variegated testicular mass
Hemorrhage and necrosis may be prominent
microscopy: Primitive pleomorphic cells in cohesive groups
Overlapping nuclei with prominent nucleoli
Brisk mitoses and variable glandular or papillary architecture
clinical: Usually presents in young adults
Lymphovascular invasion and other tumour components require assessment
examTips: Sample a germ-cell tumour carefully because a small mixed component can alter classification.

differentials.name: Seminoma
differentials.distinction: Typically has more uniform cells, fibrous septa and a different immunophenotype.

stains: CD30 and OCT4 support embryonal carcinoma
Keratin is often positive

name: Yolk sac tumour
definition: A malignant germ-cell tumour showing extraembryonic yolk-sac differentiation.
pathogenesis: Neoplastic germ cells develop varied yolk-sac-type patterns. Pure childhood tumours and postpubertal tumours within mixed lesions have different clinicopathological contexts.
gross: A soft yellow-white or variegated mass
Hemorrhage or cystic change may occur
microscopy: Reticular or microcystic patterns are common
Schiller–Duval bodies may be present
Hyaline globules can occur
clinical: Can be associated with elevated serum AFP
Occurs in gonadal and extragonadal sites
examTips: Schiller–Duval bodies are characteristic when present, but absence does not exclude the diagnosis.

differentials.name: Other germ-cell tumours
differentials.distinction: May coexist in a mixed lesion and require broad sampling and marker correlation.

stains: AFP and glypican-3 can support yolk-sac differentiation
SALL4 supports germ-cell lineage in context

name: Mature cystic teratoma
definition: A usually benign ovarian germ-cell tumour containing mature tissues from more than one germ layer.
pathogenesis: Germ cells differentiate along multiple somatic tissue lineages. In the ovary, mature tissues commonly form a cystic lesion containing skin-associated structures.
gross: A cyst containing sebaceous material and hair
Teeth, bone or a mural protuberance can occur
microscopy: Mature squamous epithelium with skin adnexa
Variable mature cartilage, neural or other tissue
No immature neuroepithelial component in an ordinary mature teratoma
clinical: Can present as an adnexal mass
Torsion is a recognized complication
examTips: Mature ovarian teratoma and postpubertal testicular teratoma have different biological implications.

differentials.name: Immature teratoma
differentials.distinction: Contains immature tissue, especially neuroepithelium, rather than only mature components.

name: Uterine leiomyoma
definition: A benign smooth-muscle tumour of the uterus.
pathogenesis: Clonal smooth-muscle proliferation is influenced by the hormonal environment. Different locations and patterns of degeneration determine symptoms and gross appearance.
gross: A firm well-circumscribed whorled white mass
Degenerative hyalinization, cystic change or calcification may occur
microscopy: Intersecting fascicles of bland smooth-muscle cells
Elongated cigar-shaped nuclei
Ordinary lesions lack a combination of marked atypia, high mitotic activity and coagulative tumour-cell necrosis
clinical: Can cause bleeding, pressure symptoms or infertility depending on location
Many are incidental
examTips: Distinguish tumour-cell necrosis from infarct-type degeneration when evaluating an atypical smooth-muscle tumour.

differentials.name: Leiomyosarcoma
differentials.distinction: Assessment integrates atypia, mitotic activity and tumour-cell necrosis rather than size alone.

stains: Desmin and smooth-muscle actin support smooth-muscle differentiation when needed

name: Endometriosis
definition: Endometrial-type glands and stroma outside the normal uterine endometrial location.
pathogenesis: Several mechanisms may contribute to ectopic implantation or differentiation. Cyclical bleeding and inflammation can produce fibrosis, adhesions and hemosiderin accumulation.
gross: Dark hemorrhagic implants or fibrotic nodules
An ovarian endometriotic cyst can contain old brown blood
microscopy: Endometrial-type glands and stroma
Hemosiderin-laden macrophages may be present
Fibrosis and hemorrhage vary with the lesion
clinical: Can be associated with cyclic pain or infertility
The microscopic components may be sparse in old or treated lesions
examTips: Look for both glands and stroma; pigment-laden macrophages alone are not always sufficient.

differentials.name: Endosalpingiosis
differentials.distinction: Has benign tubal-type epithelium rather than the usual endometrial gland–stroma combination.

stains: CD10 can highlight endometrial-type stroma in suitable cases

name: Endometrial hyperplasia
definition: An endometrial glandular proliferation with an increased gland-to-stroma ratio, assessed for cytologic atypia.
pathogenesis: Unopposed estrogenic stimulation can promote glandular proliferation. Atypical lesions require separate assessment because they carry different associations with concurrent or subsequent carcinoma.
gross: The endometrium may be thickened
A focal polypoid pattern may occur
microscopy: Increased gland crowding relative to stroma
Variable glandular dilation and architectural complexity
Cytologic atypia distinguishes important diagnostic groups
clinical: Often presents with abnormal uterine bleeding
Clinical exposure and sampling context affect interpretation
examTips: Complex architecture alone is not the same as cytologic atypia, and current terminology must be applied consistently.

differentials.name: Well-differentiated endometrioid carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Shows features of carcinoma such as confluent or destructive glandular growth in the appropriate context.

name: Endometrioid carcinoma of endometrium
definition: A malignant endometrial epithelial tumour with endometrioid glandular differentiation.
pathogenesis: Many cases arise in a background of altered estrogen signaling and precursor glandular lesions, although molecular groups differ. Invasive growth can extend into myometrium and beyond.
gross: A polypoid or infiltrative endometrial mass
Myometrial invasion may be visible in a sectioned uterus
microscopy: Crowded malignant endometrioid glands
Variable solid growth and squamous differentiation
Myometrial or lymphovascular invasion may be present
clinical: Often presents with abnormal uterine bleeding
Molecular classification provides additional prognostic information
examTips: Grade and stage describe different aspects of the tumour; invasion depth is a staging feature.

differentials.name: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia / EIN
differentials.distinction: May be gland-crowded and atypical but lacks convincing carcinoma features.

imageQueries: Endometrioid carcinoma of endometrium gross pathology

name: Cervical squamous intraepithelial lesion
definition: An HPV-associated squamous precursor lesion of the cervix graded by its epithelial maturation and atypia.
pathogenesis: Persistent high-risk HPV infection can disrupt cell-cycle regulation. Progressive abnormalities in maturation produce low- or high-grade intraepithelial patterns.
gross: Often no grossly specific lesion
Colposcopic abnormalities guide targeted sampling
microscopy: Koilocytic change can occur in low-grade lesions
High-grade lesions show greater loss of maturation and atypia
There is no stromal invasion in an intraepithelial lesion
clinical: Detected through cervical screening and diagnostic evaluation
Persistence and grade influence clinical significance
examTips: Distinguish true koilocytosis from benign perinuclear clearing using the nuclear abnormalities.

differentials.name: Reactive squamous atypia
differentials.distinction: Can accompany inflammation but lacks the full architectural and cytologic pattern of a true lesion.

stains: Block-type p16 staining supports transforming HPV-associated high-grade lesions in the proper setting
imageQueries: Cervical squamous intraepithelial lesion gross pathology

name: Squamous cell carcinoma of cervix
definition: An invasive malignant squamous epithelial tumour of the uterine cervix.
pathogenesis: Persistent oncogenic HPV infection is central to many cases. Intraepithelial neoplasia can progress to stromal invasion, with subsequent local and metastatic spread.
gross: An exophytic, ulcerated or infiltrative cervical lesion
Advanced disease may distort adjacent tissues
microscopy: Infiltrating nests or cords of atypical squamous cells
Variable keratinization and intercellular bridges
Stromal reaction and lymphovascular invasion may occur
clinical: Can cause abnormal bleeding or discharge
Stage requires clinical and pathological integration
examTips: A superficial sample may underrepresent invasion; evaluate the epithelial–stromal interface carefully.

differentials.name: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
differentials.distinction: Has severe epithelial atypia without established stromal invasion.

stains: p16 can support an HPV-associated process
Squamous markers are useful in selected difficult tumours
imageQueries: Squamous cell carcinoma of cervix histopathology
Squamous cell carcinoma of cervix gross pathology

references.title: Libre Pathology: Squamous cell carcinoma of the uterine cervix

name: High-grade serous carcinoma
definition: An aggressive tubo-ovarian or peritoneal epithelial carcinoma with marked atypia and serous-type differentiation.
pathogenesis: Many cases originate from precursor lesions in the fimbrial fallopian tube. TP53 abnormalities and, in a subset, homologous-recombination defects are important molecular features.
gross: Complex solid and cystic masses
Papillary excrescences and peritoneal deposits can occur
microscopy: Marked nuclear atypia and brisk mitotic activity
Papillary, solid or slit-like glandular architecture
Psammoma bodies may occur but are not obligatory
clinical: Often presents with advanced abdominal disease
The primary site is assigned using integrated anatomical and pathological findings
examTips: High-grade and low-grade serous carcinomas are biologically distinct categories.

differentials.name: Low-grade serous carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Usually has less nuclear atypia and a different molecular pathway.

stains: WT1 and PAX8 support Mullerian serous differentiation
An aberrant p53 pattern is common

references.title: Libre Pathology: serous carcinoma of the ovary

name: Ovarian mucinous tumour
definition: An ovarian epithelial tumour with mucinous differentiation, classified as benign, borderline or malignant by defined features.
pathogenesis: Mucinous epithelium proliferates within cystic ovarian lesions. The distinction between primary ovarian disease and metastatic mucinous tumour is critical, especially for bilateral or infiltrative lesions.
gross: Often a large multilocular cyst with mucinous contents
Solid or irregular areas require extensive sampling
microscopy: Mucin-producing columnar epithelium
Epithelial stratification and atypia vary by category
Confluent or destructive stromal invasion supports carcinoma
clinical: Can present as an adnexal mass
Clinical evaluation must consider a gastrointestinal primary
examTips: A single bland section cannot classify a large heterogeneous mucinous tumour.

differentials.name: Metastatic gastrointestinal carcinoma
differentials.distinction: May mimic an ovarian mucinous primary and requires integrated clinical, gross and marker assessment.

stains: CK7, CK20, CDX2 and SATB2 are interpreted as a panel when needed

name: Hydatidiform mole
definition: An abnormal gestation with hydropic chorionic villi and trophoblastic proliferation, classified as complete or partial.
pathogenesis: Abnormal genomic contributions at conception generate characteristic gestational patterns. Complete and partial moles differ in genetic background, morphology and ancillary findings.
gross: Swollen translucent chorionic villi can resemble tiny vesicles
The amount of fetal tissue depends on the type and sampling
microscopy: Hydropic villi with cistern formation in many cases
Trophoblastic proliferation differs in distribution and degree
Villous shape and fetal elements help assess the differential
clinical: Can be associated with abnormal bleeding and elevated hCG
Follow-up is important because persistent trophoblastic disease can occur
examTips: Early gestations may not show a fully developed classic appearance; use ancillary studies appropriately.

differentials.name: Hydropic nonmolar abortion
differentials.distinction: Can have swollen villi without the full molar pattern.

stains: p57 nuclear staining is usually absent in villous stroma and cytotrophoblast of complete moles, and retained in partial and nonmolar gestations
p57 alone cannot distinguish a partial mole from a nonmolar gestation
Genotyping can resolve difficult cases

name: Choriocarcinoma
definition: A malignant trophoblastic tumour composed of malignant trophoblast without chorionic villi.
pathogenesis: Gestational cases arise from a prior pregnancy, while nongestational cases can occur in germ-cell tumours. Proliferative trophoblast invades vessels and produces extensive hemorrhage.
gross: A hemorrhagic necrotic mass
Metastatic deposits may also be markedly hemorrhagic
microscopy: Malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast
Extensive hemorrhage and necrosis
Chorionic villi are absent in pure choriocarcinoma
clinical: Often associated with elevated hCG
Gestational context and genetics help establish the origin
examTips: Absence of villi distinguishes the classic lesion from an invasive mole containing villous structures.

differentials.name: Other gestational trophoblastic tumours
differentials.distinction: Have different trophoblastic cell compositions and immunophenotypes.

stains: hCG highlights syncytiotrophoblastic differentiation in an appropriate panel

name: Fibroadenoma
definition: A benign biphasic breast tumour composed of epithelial and stromal elements.
pathogenesis: Stromal proliferation distorts and surrounds benign ductal structures. The interaction of the two components produces pericanalicular and intracanalicular patterns.
gross: A well-circumscribed rubbery mobile mass
A pale lobulated cut surface with slit-like spaces
microscopy: Bland stromal proliferation
Compressed or open benign ducts
Ducts retain epithelial and myoepithelial layers
clinical: Commonly presents as a palpable mass in younger patients
Clinical imaging findings guide sampling
examTips: Assess stromal cellularity and architecture when distinguishing a fibroadenoma from a phyllodes tumour.

differentials.name: Phyllodes tumour
differentials.distinction: Often has more prominent leaf-like architecture and a more cellular stromal component.

name: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type
definition: An invasive breast epithelial malignancy lacking the defining features of a recognized special histologic type.
pathogenesis: Accumulated epithelial molecular alterations permit growth beyond the duct–lobular system into stroma. Receptor status and other biomarkers add important biological information.
gross: An irregular firm stellate mass is common
Skin or nipple retraction can occur with local tissue involvement
microscopy: Infiltrating malignant glands, nests or cords
Desmoplastic stromal response
Nuclear grade and tubule formation vary
clinical: May present as a mass or imaging abnormality
Grade, stage and biomarker results have distinct roles
examTips: Invasive ductal carcinoma is a familiar historical name, but no-special-type terminology is more precise for this category.

differentials.name: Invasive lobular carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Typically has a discohesive growth pattern and different cell-adhesion findings.

stains: ER, PR and HER2 are clinically important biomarkers
Myoepithelial markers assist selected in-situ versus invasive differentials
imageQueries: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type histopathology
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type gross pathology

references.title: Libre Pathology: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast

name: Invasive lobular carcinoma
definition: An invasive breast carcinoma typically composed of discohesive cells due to altered cell adhesion.
pathogenesis: Loss of functional E-cadherin-associated adhesion is characteristic of classic disease. Discohesive cells infiltrate stroma in subtle single-cell patterns.
gross: May be an ill-defined thickening rather than a sharply defined mass
Gross extent can be difficult to appreciate
microscopy: Single-file infiltration by discohesive cells
Targetoid growth around ducts may occur
Classic cells can appear relatively bland
clinical: Can be multifocal or bilateral
Imaging and gross assessment may underestimate extent
examTips: Bland nuclei do not exclude an invasive lobular carcinoma.

differentials.name: Invasive carcinoma of no special type
differentials.distinction: Usually shows greater cohesion and retained membranous E-cadherin in typical cases.

stains: E-cadherin and p120 patterns support the diagnosis in context

name: Ductal carcinoma in situ
definition: A neoplastic epithelial proliferation confined to the breast duct–lobular system without stromal invasion.
pathogenesis: Clonal epithelial alterations produce intraductal neoplasia of variable grade and architecture. Progression to invasion can occur, but risk varies among lesions.
gross: May be grossly occult
Calcifications or a localized lesion can guide imaging detection
microscopy: Ducts expanded by atypical epithelial cells
Cribriform, solid, papillary or other patterns
Necrosis and calcification may occur; a peripheral myoepithelial layer remains
clinical: Frequently detected on mammography
Extent, grade and margin assessment are important
examTips: Comedonecrosis is a morphological feature and can occur within high-grade in-situ disease; it does not itself prove invasion.

differentials.name: Invasive carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Breaches the confines of the duct–lobular unit into stroma.

stains: Myoepithelial markers can help in selected difficult cases
imageQueries: Ductal carcinoma in situ gross pathology

references.title: Libre Pathology: Ductal carcinoma in situ

name: Fibrocystic change
definition: A descriptive group of common benign breast alterations including cysts, fibrosis and epithelial changes.
pathogenesis: Hormonal and involutional influences contribute to variable changes in the terminal duct–lobular units. The significance depends on whether a specific proliferative or atypical lesion is also present.
gross: Cysts and firm fibrotic areas
Some cysts have a blue-domed appearance
microscopy: Cystically dilated ducts
Apocrine metaplasia and stromal fibrosis
Associated epithelial hyperplasia may be present
clinical: Can present with nodularity or pain
The umbrella term does not replace identification of a clinically relevant specific lesion
examTips: Separate ordinary benign change from atypical proliferative lesions with different implications.

differentials.name: Fibroadenoma
differentials.distinction: Is a circumscribed biphasic neoplasm rather than a diffuse collection of benign changes.

name: Hashimoto thyroiditis
definition: An autoimmune thyroiditis with lymphocytic destruction and variable follicular atrophy.
pathogenesis: Immune-mediated injury targets thyroid tissue. Progressive follicular loss can reduce thyroid function and induce compensatory epithelial change.
gross: The thyroid can be diffusely enlarged and firm
Late disease may be atrophic
microscopy: Dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with lymphoid follicles
Follicular atrophy
Oncocytic follicular-cell change is common
clinical: Often associated with hypothyroidism
Clinical thyroid-function and antibody findings support the context
examTips: Oncocytic cells alone do not establish an oncocytic neoplasm.

differentials.name: Thyroid lymphoma
differentials.distinction: Can arise in this setting and requires assessment of a monomorphic destructive lymphoid proliferation.

name: Graves disease
definition: An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating antibodies produce diffuse glandular hyperfunction.
pathogenesis: Antibodies activate the TSH receptor and stimulate follicular-cell growth and hormone production. The diffuse hyperplastic response changes follicular architecture and colloid.
gross: A diffusely enlarged vascular thyroid
The gland is usually not dominated by one encapsulated nodule
microscopy: Tall crowded follicular cells
Papillary infoldings without the defining nuclear features of papillary carcinoma
Scalloped colloid can be prominent
clinical: Produces a clinical hyperthyroid syndrome
Eye and other extrathyroidal manifestations can occur
examTips: Papillary infoldings in hyperfunction are not equivalent to papillary thyroid carcinoma.

differentials.name: Papillary thyroid carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Has a characteristic constellation of nuclear abnormalities and a different growth context.

name: Follicular adenoma of thyroid
definition: A benign encapsulated follicular-cell neoplasm without capsular or vascular invasion.
pathogenesis: A clonal follicular-cell proliferation forms a discrete nodule. Classification depends on excluding invasive growth through careful assessment of the tumour–capsule interface.
gross: A solitary well-circumscribed encapsulated nodule
The cut surface may differ from adjacent thyroid
microscopy: Follicular architecture with variable colloid
A discrete capsule around the lesion
No diagnostic capsular or vascular invasion
clinical: Often presents as a thyroid nodule
Cytology alone cannot reliably distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma
examTips: The capsule and vessels must be sampled adequately; nuclear blandness does not settle the adenoma–carcinoma distinction.

differentials.name: Follicular thyroid carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Requires diagnostic capsular or vascular invasion.

imageQueries: Follicular adenoma of thyroid gross pathology

name: Papillary thyroid carcinoma
definition: A malignant follicular-cell-derived thyroid tumour defined primarily by characteristic nuclear features.
pathogenesis: Specific signaling-pathway alterations drive distinct tumour subsets. Tumour architecture varies, so classification requires attention to nuclear features and invasion where relevant.
gross: A firm thyroid nodule
Fibrosis, calcification or multifocality may occur
microscopy: Enlarged overlapping nuclei with clearing
Nuclear grooves and intranuclear cytoplasmic pseudoinclusions
Papillae or psammoma bodies may be present
clinical: Often presents as a thyroid nodule or cervical node
Clinical behavior varies with variant and stage
examTips: Papillary architecture alone is insufficient; the nuclear constellation is central.

differentials.name: Benign papillary hyperplasia
differentials.distinction: Can form papillary folds without the full characteristic nuclear changes.

stains: Thyroglobulin and TTF-1 support follicular-cell origin when needed

name: Follicular thyroid carcinoma
definition: An invasive follicular-cell thyroid carcinoma lacking the defining nuclear pattern of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
pathogenesis: A follicular-patterned neoplasm acquires the ability to invade its capsule or vessels. The pattern and extent of invasion are central to pathological classification.
gross: Often an encapsulated or partly encapsulated thyroid mass
Hemorrhage or degenerative change can occur
microscopy: Follicular growth pattern
Diagnostic capsular or vascular invasion
Papillary-type nuclear features are absent or insufficient for that diagnosis
clinical: Can spread through blood vessels
Cytology cannot establish the required invasive criterion
examTips: Do not diagnose follicular carcinoma solely from cellularity or cytologic atypia on a needle sample.

differentials.name: Follicular adenoma
differentials.distinction: Has no diagnostic capsular or vascular invasion after adequate sampling.

name: Medullary thyroid carcinoma
definition: A neuroendocrine thyroid carcinoma derived from parafollicular C cells.
pathogenesis: RET-associated hereditary pathways account for an important subset, while sporadic cases also occur. Neoplastic C cells produce calcitonin and may deposit peptide-derived amyloid.
gross: A firm thyroid mass
Hereditary cases may be multifocal or bilateral
microscopy: Nests or trabeculae of neuroendocrine cells
Plasmacytoid or spindle-cell forms can occur
Amyloid may be present in the stroma
clinical: Can be associated with hereditary endocrine neoplasia syndromes
Serum calcitonin and genetic context are important
examTips: Stromal amyloid is a clue but should be confirmed and integrated with tumour markers.

differentials.name: Other neuroendocrine neoplasms
differentials.distinction: Require lineage and site assessment rather than neuroendocrine morphology alone.

stains: Calcitonin supports C-cell differentiation
Congo red demonstrates associated amyloid when present

name: Pheochromocytoma
definition: An adrenal medullary neuroendocrine neoplasm of chromaffin cells.
pathogenesis: Alterations in several hereditary and sporadic pathways can promote chromaffin-cell proliferation. Catecholamine production produces important physiological effects in functioning tumours.
gross: A well-circumscribed adrenal mass
Hemorrhage or cystic degeneration may occur
microscopy: Nested zellballen architecture
Granular neuroendocrine cytoplasm
A rich vascular network and supporting sustentacular cells
clinical: May cause episodic catecholamine-related symptoms
Hereditary associations require clinical consideration
examTips: Histology alone cannot reliably declare a pheochromocytoma biologically benign; metastatic disease defines metastatic behavior.

differentials.name: Adrenal cortical neoplasm
differentials.distinction: Has different lineage markers and often a different cytoplasmic and architectural pattern.

stains: Chromogranin and synaptophysin support neuroendocrine differentiation
S100 or SOX10 can highlight sustentacular cells

name: Parathyroid adenoma
definition: A benign usually single-gland parathyroid neoplasm that can cause primary hyperparathyroidism.
pathogenesis: Clonal parathyroid-cell proliferation increases hormone secretion in functioning lesions. The distinction from multigland disease requires clinical and operative context as well as pathology.
gross: An enlarged circumscribed parathyroid gland
A rim of relatively normal parathyroid may be present
microscopy: Hypercellular chief-cell or other parathyroid-cell proliferation
Reduced stromal fat relative to appropriate normal tissue
A capsule or compressed peripheral tissue may be seen
clinical: Can be associated with hypercalcemia and its systemic effects
Some cases are found during biochemical evaluation
examTips: An isolated hypercellular gland cannot always distinguish adenoma from hyperplasia without the operative context.

differentials.name: Parathyroid hyperplasia
differentials.distinction: Often involves multiple glands, although size and involvement can be uneven.

stains: PTH supports parathyroid lineage in selected difficult cases

name: Osteomyelitis
definition: Inflammation of bone and marrow, usually caused by infection.
pathogenesis: Organisms reach bone through blood, direct inoculation or contiguous spread. Persistent infection can devitalize bone and provoke reactive new-bone formation.
gross: Pus or necrotic bone may be present
Chronic lesions can contain a sequestrum within reactive new bone
microscopy: Neutrophilic inflammation in acute disease
Necrotic bone with empty osteocyte lacunae
Chronic inflammation, fibrosis and reactive bone in longstanding disease
clinical: May cause pain, fever or a draining sinus
Cultures and the route of infection help determine the cause
examTips: Sequestrum is devitalized bone; involucrum is surrounding reactive new bone.

differentials.name: Bone tumour
differentials.distinction: Can produce destructive imaging findings, so correlate infection studies, imaging and histology.

stains: Organism stains are selected from the clinical differential and do not replace culture

references.title: Libre Pathology: acute and chronic osteomyelitis

name: Osteosarcoma
definition: A malignant mesenchymal tumour defined by production of osteoid by malignant cells.
pathogenesis: Molecular abnormalities allow malignant osteoblastic differentiation. The amount of osteoid and the accompanying stromal pattern vary considerably across subtypes.
gross: A destructive bone mass with variable gritty mineralization
Soft-tissue extension, hemorrhage and necrosis can occur
microscopy: Atypical malignant cells directly associated with osteoid
Variable osteoblastic, chondroblastic or fibroblastic patterns
Mitotic activity can be brisk in conventional high-grade disease
clinical: Often arises near the knee in adolescents, but other age groups and sites occur
Imaging–histology correlation is essential
examTips: Malignant osteoid production, not just any bone in a tumour, is the key defining feature.

differentials.name: Reactive callus
differentials.distinction: Can be cellular but shows an appropriate maturation pattern and clinical setting.

name: Chondrosarcoma
definition: A malignant mesenchymal tumour with cartilaginous differentiation.
pathogenesis: Neoplastic cartilage proliferates and can permeate pre-existing bone. Different molecular and morphological subtypes have different biological behavior.
gross: A lobulated cartilage-like mass
Calcification and myxoid or cystic change may be present
microscopy: Lobules of neoplastic cartilage
Cellularity and nuclear atypia vary with grade
Permeation of host bone helps establish malignancy in appropriate lesions
clinical: Often presents with pain or an enlarging bone lesion
Radiologic location and growth pattern are central to diagnosis
examTips: Binucleated chondrocytes alone do not prove malignancy.

differentials.name: Enchondroma
differentials.distinction: Can contain atypical-looking cartilage; assessment depends on site, imaging and host-bone relationships.

name: Giant cell tumour of bone
definition: A generally locally aggressive bone neoplasm with mononuclear neoplastic cells and numerous osteoclast-like giant cells.
pathogenesis: The neoplastic stromal component recruits osteoclast-lineage cells and promotes bone resorption. The resulting lesion often approaches the articular surface in skeletally mature patients.
gross: An expansile brown-red lytic lesion
Hemorrhage or secondary cystic change may occur
microscopy: Numerous osteoclast-like giant cells
Mononuclear cells with nuclei resembling those in the giant cells
Giant cells are distributed relatively evenly in typical areas
clinical: Classically involves an epiphyseal region after skeletal maturity
Local recurrence and rare metastatic behavior are recognized
examTips: The giant cells are not the principal neoplastic population.

differentials.name: Brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism
differentials.distinction: Can look similar; biochemical findings and context are decisive.

stains: H3.3 G34W immunostaining can support many conventional cases
imageQueries: Giant cell tumour of bone histopathology
Giant cell tumour of bone gross pathology

references.title: Libre Pathology: Giant cell tumour of bone

name: Ewing sarcoma
definition: A malignant small-round-cell sarcoma characterized by a compatible fusion-associated molecular profile.
pathogenesis: A characteristic transcription-factor fusion drives the tumour phenotype. Primitive cells proliferate in bone or soft tissue and can produce a destructive mass.
gross: A soft gray-white destructive mass
Hemorrhage and necrosis may be present
microscopy: Sheets of relatively uniform small round cells
Scant clear or pale cytoplasm
Necrosis and reactive changes can complicate limited samples
clinical: Often occurs in children or young adults
Clinical and imaging findings overlap with other tumours and infection
examTips: CD99 positivity alone is not specific enough to establish Ewing sarcoma.

differentials.name: Lymphoblastic lymphoma
differentials.distinction: May also be a small-round-cell tumour and requires lineage assessment.

stains: Strong membranous CD99 is supportive in context
Molecular confirmation distinguishes Ewing sarcoma from related round-cell sarcomas

name: Basal cell carcinoma
definition: A locally invasive skin carcinoma with basaloid differentiation, commonly associated with ultraviolet exposure.
pathogenesis: Hedgehog-pathway dysregulation contributes to tumorigenesis in many cases. Growth is usually locally destructive rather than widely metastatic.
gross: A pearly papule, plaque or ulcerated lesion
Clinical appearance varies by subtype
microscopy: Nests of basaloid cells
Peripheral palisading
Clefting between tumour nests and surrounding stroma is common in conventional lesions
clinical: Often occurs on sun-exposed skin
Local extent and histologic subtype affect behavior
examTips: Palisading and retraction are useful clues, but interpret them within the full tumour pattern.

differentials.name: Trichoepithelioma
differentials.distinction: A benign follicular tumour that can mimic basal cell carcinoma and may require a careful architectural assessment.

stains: BerEP4 can support basal-cell differentiation in selected differentials

name: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
definition: An invasive malignant squamous epithelial tumour of the skin.
pathogenesis: Ultraviolet damage, immunosuppression and chronic injury can contribute to tumorigenesis. Neoplastic keratinocytes invade dermis and sometimes deeper structures.
gross: A scaly, keratotic or ulcerated lesion
An infiltrative mass may develop
microscopy: Atypical squamous nests infiltrating dermis
Keratin pearls or individual-cell keratinization may occur
Intercellular bridges can support differentiation
clinical: Often arises on sun-damaged skin
Some tumours have increased risk of recurrence or metastasis based on specific features
examTips: A keratinizing surface lesion needs assessment of the base to evaluate invasion.

differentials.name: Keratoacanthoma-type lesion
differentials.distinction: May closely resemble well-differentiated carcinoma; architecture and adequate sampling matter.

stains: p40 or keratins can assist selected poorly differentiated lesions
imageQueries: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma gross pathology

references.title: Libre Pathology: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

name: Melanoma
definition: A malignant neoplasm of melanocytes with variable architectural and cytologic appearances.
pathogenesis: Genetic alterations interact with exposure and host factors in different melanoma subtypes. Tumour cells can spread within epidermis and invade dermis with metastatic potential.
gross: An asymmetric variably pigmented lesion may be present
Some melanomas are amelanotic
microscopy: Asymmetric atypical melanocytic proliferation
Pagetoid epidermal spread can occur
Dermal invasion with impaired maturation supports an invasive lesion
clinical: Can arise in cutaneous, mucosal or other melanocytic sites
Breslow thickness is important for invasive cutaneous melanoma assessment
examTips: Pigment is not required; an amelanotic lesion can still be melanoma.

differentials.name: Melanocytic nevus
differentials.distinction: Usually has greater symmetry, orderly architecture and maturation, although difficult variants exist.

stains: SOX10 and S100 support melanocytic lineage
Melan-A and other markers are interpreted in a panel

name: Psoriasis
definition: A chronic immune-mediated skin disease with a characteristic but variable psoriasiform tissue-reaction pattern.
pathogenesis: Immune signaling accelerates epidermal turnover and sustains inflammation. Abnormal keratinization and vascular changes contribute to the plaque phenotype.
gross: Well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques
Distribution and appearance depend on clinical subtype and treatment
microscopy: Regular psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia
Parakeratosis and reduced granular layer
Neutrophils in the stratum corneum or superficial epidermis may occur
clinical: Often follows a relapsing course
Clinical correlation is necessary because other disorders share psoriasiform changes
examTips: Treated lesions may lack textbook features; a psoriasiform pattern is not automatically psoriasis.

differentials.name: Chronic spongiotic dermatitis
differentials.distinction: Can show epidermal hyperplasia but often has more prominent spongiosis and a different clinical setting.

stains: PAS may help exclude a fungal mimic when indicated

name: Pemphigus vulgaris
definition: An autoimmune blistering disease with intraepidermal acantholysis, often affecting mucosa as well as skin.
pathogenesis: Autoantibodies against desmosomal adhesion proteins disrupt keratinocyte cohesion. The resulting split typically develops above the basal cell layer.
gross: Fragile flaccid blisters and erosions
Mucosal erosions can be prominent
microscopy: Suprabasal acantholysis
Basal keratinocytes remain attached to the basement-membrane region
Detached acantholytic cells occur within the cleft
clinical: Can produce painful mucocutaneous erosions
Routine histology and perilesional immunofluorescence provide complementary evidence
examTips: Biopsy site matters: a fully eroded lesion may not preserve the diagnostic cleavage plane.

differentials.name: Bullous pemphigoid
differentials.distinction: Has a subepidermal rather than suprabasal split and a different immunofluorescence pattern.

stains: Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG and often C3 in an appropriate sample

name: Meningioma
definition: A usually dural-based neoplasm with meningothelial differentiation and a range of histologic grades.
pathogenesis: Molecular alterations in meningothelial-lineage cells produce a slowly or more rapidly growing mass depending on tumour type. Anatomical location strongly influences clinical effects.
gross: A firm dural-attached mass
A whorled cut surface or calcification may be present
microscopy: Meningothelial cells forming whorls
Psammoma bodies may occur
Nuclear pseudoinclusions are a useful feature in some tumours
clinical: Often causes compression rather than diffuse parenchymal infiltration
Clinical behavior depends on site and grade
examTips: Whorls and psammoma bodies are suggestive but must be interpreted with the entire lesion.

differentials.name: Schwannoma
differentials.distinction: Has a different alternating architecture and neural-crest marker profile.

stains: EMA and somatostatin-receptor markers can support meningothelial differentiation

name: Schwannoma
definition: A usually benign peripheral nerve-sheath neoplasm composed of Schwann cells.
pathogenesis: Clonal Schwann-cell proliferation forms a circumscribed tumour associated with a nerve. Sporadic and syndromic settings have different clinical implications.
gross: A circumscribed often encapsulated mass
Larger tumours may show cystic degeneration or hemorrhage
microscopy: Alternating cellular Antoni A and loose Antoni B areas
Nuclear palisading can form Verocay bodies
Hyalinized vessels may be conspicuous
clinical: Can present as a nerve-associated mass
Vestibular lesions have important anatomical and syndromic associations
examTips: Ancient degenerative atypia can be striking without implying malignancy.

differentials.name: Neurofibroma
differentials.distinction: Usually has a less uniformly Schwann-cell population and a different relationship to the nerve.

stains: S100 and SOX10 commonly show strong Schwann-cell differentiation

name: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype
definition: An aggressive diffuse astrocytic glioma classified using integrated histologic and molecular findings.
pathogenesis: Molecular abnormalities drive infiltrative astrocytic growth in an IDH-wildtype setting. Histologic or defined molecular features establish the integrated diagnostic category.
gross: An ill-defined infiltrative cerebral mass
Necrosis and hemorrhage can create a variegated cut surface
microscopy: Markedly atypical infiltrative glial cells
Microvascular proliferation
Necrosis with pseudopalisading cells may occur
clinical: Usually presents in adults with neurological effects of an intracranial lesion
Integrated molecular classification is essential
examTips: Do not use glioblastoma as a synonym for every high-grade glioma; IDH status and other molecular findings matter.

differentials.name: Metastatic carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Can also form a necrotic brain mass but has a different lineage and growth pattern.

stains: GFAP supports glial differentiation in context
Molecular studies establish the integrated category

references.title: WHO Classification of Tumours: Central Nervous System Tumours, fifth edition (2021)

name: Pilocytic astrocytoma
definition: A circumscribed astrocytic glioma often associated with MAPK-pathway alterations.
pathogenesis: A pathway-driven glial proliferation typically produces relatively indolent local growth. Anatomical site influences presentation and the feasibility of complete assessment or excision.
gross: A circumscribed lesion that may be cystic with a mural nodule
Cerebellar lesions are familiar examples
microscopy: Biphasic compact and loose areas may be present
Piloid cells with elongated processes
Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies may occur
clinical: Often occurs in children or young people
Some cases are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1
examTips: Rosenthal fibres are not unique to this tumour and can occur in chronic reactive gliosis.

differentials.name: Diffuse astrocytic glioma
differentials.distinction: Usually has a more infiltrative growth pattern and different integrated molecular classification.

stains: GFAP supports glial differentiation
MAPK-pathway studies can aid classification

name: Medulloblastoma
definition: A malignant embryonal tumour of the cerebellum, classified into molecularly and histologically distinct groups.
pathogenesis: Developmental signaling abnormalities drive primitive neuroepithelial proliferation. The tumour can disseminate through cerebrospinal-fluid pathways.
gross: A soft cerebellar mass
Necrosis or hemorrhage may be present
microscopy: Densely packed primitive small cells
High mitotic and apoptotic activity
Homer Wright-type rosettes may occur
clinical: Often presents in childhood with posterior-fossa symptoms
Molecular group is important for integrated classification
examTips: A small-round-cell cerebellar tumour requires integrated classification rather than morphology alone.

differentials.name: Other embryonal CNS tumours
differentials.distinction: Can overlap histologically and require molecular and immunophenotypic evaluation.

stains: Synaptophysin can support neuronal differentiation in context

name: Cerebral infarction
definition: Ischemic brain-tissue death caused by inadequate perfusion.
pathogenesis: Arterial occlusion or severe hypoperfusion deprives neurons and glia of oxygen and substrates. Enzymatic digestion and macrophage clearance lead to liquefaction and eventual cavitation.
gross: A swollen softened region early
An old infarct can leave a cystic cavity
microscopy: Acute ischemic neuronal change may include red neurons
Neutrophils are followed by macrophages
Gliosis develops at the lesion margin as dead tissue is cleared
clinical: Can cause focal neurological deficits
Clinical timing and reperfusion alter the tissue appearance
examTips: The brain typically undergoes liquefactive rather than classic coagulative necrosis after infarction.

differentials.name: Hypoxic–ischemic injury
differentials.distinction: Can have a more diffuse or selectively vulnerable distribution rather than one arterial territory.

references.title: Libre Pathology: necrosis including ischemic brain injury

name: Alzheimer disease
definition: A neurodegenerative disorder associated with a characteristic distribution of amyloid-beta and tau-related pathology.
pathogenesis: Abnormal protein processing and aggregation contribute to synaptic and neuronal dysfunction. The pattern and burden of pathology must be integrated with clinical cognitive findings.
gross: Cerebral cortical atrophy with widened sulci
Ventricular enlargement can reflect loss of brain volume
microscopy: Amyloid-beta plaques
Tau-positive neurofibrillary tangles and neuropil threads
Neuronal loss and gliosis in affected regions
clinical: A common cause of progressive dementia
Other pathologies can coexist and contribute to impairment
examTips: Plaques or tangles in isolation do not define the clinical cause of every dementia.

differentials.name: Lewy body disease
differentials.distinction: Has a different key protein-deposition pattern, although mixed pathology is possible.

stains: Amyloid-beta and phospho-tau immunohistochemistry characterize the deposits

name: Leprosy
definition: A chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae or M. lepromatosis with important skin and peripheral-nerve involvement.
pathogenesis: The host cellular immune response shapes the disease spectrum. Stronger cellular responses favour granulomatous lesions, whereas poor containment can allow numerous organisms in macrophages.
gross: Skin plaques or nodules with variable distribution
Peripheral-nerve involvement can cause characteristic deformity over time
microscopy: Tuberculoid disease shows granulomatous inflammation with few bacilli
Lepromatous disease has foamy macrophages with many organisms
Nerve involvement is a useful clue when present
clinical: Sensory loss and nerve disease are clinically important
The morphological spectrum requires clinical correlation
examTips: Organism burden and granuloma formation vary inversely across much of the spectrum.

differentials.name: Other granulomatous skin disease
differentials.distinction: Requires careful assessment of nerves, organisms and clinical distribution.

stains: Fite stain is useful for demonstrating lepra bacilli

name: Candidiasis
definition: Infection by Candida species, producing superficial or invasive disease depending on host and site.
pathogenesis: Mucosal barrier disruption, altered flora or impaired immunity can permit fungal overgrowth or invasion. Tissue invasion provokes variable inflammatory and necrotic injury.
gross: White mucosal plaques may occur in superficial disease
Invasive disease may form necrotic foci in organs
microscopy: Budding yeasts and pseudohyphae in typical cases
Organisms can involve necrotic surface debris or invade tissue
Neutrophilic inflammation is common but host-dependent
clinical: Can be superficial or disseminated
Demonstrating organisms on a surface is not identical to proving invasive infection
examTips: Assess the relationship of fungi to tissue rather than only noting their presence.

differentials.name: Other fungal infection
differentials.distinction: Morphology overlaps, and culture or molecular studies may be needed for reliable species identification.

stains: GMS and PAS highlight fungal forms

name: Aspergillosis
definition: Disease caused by Aspergillus species, ranging from colonization and allergy to invasive infection.
pathogenesis: Inhaled spores can grow in a susceptible pulmonary environment. In immunocompromised patients, tissue and vascular invasion can produce infarction and hemorrhage.
gross: A fungal ball may occupy a pre-existing cavity
Invasive disease can produce hemorrhagic necrotic lesions
microscopy: Septate hyphae with relatively acute-angle branching in typical sections
Tissue invasion in invasive disease
Angioinvasion can cause thrombosis and necrosis
clinical: Host immune status strongly affects the pattern
A fungal ball does not by itself establish tissue-invasive disease
examTips: Branching morphology suggests a group of fungi; definitive species identification needs appropriate microbiology.

differentials.name: Mucormycosis
differentials.distinction: Typically shows broader irregular pauciseptate hyphae, but damaged sections can overlap.

stains: GMS and PAS demonstrate fungal hyphae

name: Hydatid cyst
definition: A tissue cyst formed by the larval stage of Echinococcus species.
pathogenesis: Ingested eggs release larvae that can lodge in organs such as liver or lung. The parasite forms a cyst with host-derived fibrous reaction and characteristic parasite structures.
gross: A cystic lesion with a pale wall
Daughter cysts and hydatid sand may be present
microscopy: Acellular laminated parasite membrane
An inner germinal layer may be preserved
Brood capsules, protoscolices or hooklets can establish the diagnosis
clinical: Often involves liver or lung
Clinical significance depends on organ and cyst complications
examTips: An old or degenerated cyst may show only laminated material; search carefully for diagnostic structures.

differentials.name: Nonparasitic cyst
differentials.distinction: Lacks the characteristic laminated parasite membrane and protoscolices.

stains: PAS can accentuate the laminated membrane

name: Acute inflammation
definition: A rapid tissue response to injury with vascular changes, exudation and recruitment of inflammatory cells.
pathogenesis: Recognition of microbes or damaged cells activates local mediators. Vasodilation, increased permeability and leukocyte recruitment help contain and remove the insult.
gross: Redness, warmth and swelling may be visible
Exudate can be serous, fibrinous or purulent
microscopy: Dilated congested small vessels
Interstitial edema or fibrin-rich exudation
Neutrophils commonly predominate early in many injuries
clinical: Can follow infectious or noninfectious injury
Outcomes include resolution, abscess or persistent injury
examTips: Inflammation is not synonymous with infection.

differentials.name: Chronic inflammation
differentials.distinction: Often has a greater mononuclear-cell component with persistent injury and repair.

name: Chronic inflammation
definition: A persistent inflammatory response combining ongoing injury with attempts at repair.
pathogenesis: A stimulus that is not cleared or an inappropriate immune response sustains inflammation. Macrophages and lymphocytes contribute to tissue damage and fibrotic remodeling.
gross: Thickening, nodularity or fibrosis may occur
The appearance depends on the affected organ
microscopy: Mononuclear inflammatory cells are common
Tissue destruction may coexist with regeneration
Fibroblasts and collagen can be increased
clinical: Occurs with persistent infection, autoimmunity or prolonged exposure
Histology must be integrated with the clinical context
examTips: Chronic describes the response pattern rather than one etiology.

differentials.name: Acute inflammation
differentials.distinction: Typically emphasizes rapid exudation and an early neutrophilic response.

name: Type I hypersensitivity
definition: An immediate hypersensitivity mechanism driven by IgE-associated mast-cell activation in a sensitized host.
pathogenesis: Sensitization produces antigen-specific IgE that binds mast cells. Re-exposure can cross-link bound IgE and release mediators, followed in some settings by a later inflammatory phase.
gross: Edema or mucus production can occur
The appearance depends on the affected tissue
microscopy: Edema and vascular changes
Eosinophils can be prominent in late responses
Mucosal sites can show increased mucus-producing cells
clinical: Examples include allergic rhinitis and some asthma
The response can be localized or systemic
examTips: Not every eosinophil-rich lesion represents a type I allergy.

differentials.name: Type IV hypersensitivity
differentials.distinction: Is primarily T-cell mediated rather than an immediate IgE–mast-cell reaction.

name: Type II hypersensitivity
definition: Antibody-mediated injury or dysfunction directed at antigens on cells or extracellular structures.
pathogenesis: IgG or IgM binds a target and can recruit complement or effector cells. Some antibodies alter receptor function rather than directly destroying the target.
gross: Gross findings depend on the targeted tissue
Receptor-mediated disorders may have little destructive change
microscopy: The pattern depends on the target
Cell destruction or inflammation can occur
Selected diseases have characteristic immunofluorescence patterns
clinical: Examples include some immune cytopenias and receptor-directed autoimmunity
Mechanism and clinical diagnosis are distinct concepts
examTips: Type II includes functional antibody effects as well as cytotoxic injury.

differentials.name: Type III hypersensitivity
differentials.distinction: Primarily involves tissue deposition of immune complexes.

name: Type III hypersensitivity
definition: Immune-complex-mediated tissue injury associated with complement activation and inflammatory recruitment.
pathogenesis: Antigen–antibody complexes accumulate in susceptible sites. Complement and recruited cells then injure vessel walls or other tissues.
gross: Tissues may be swollen or hemorrhagic
Kidney, skin or joints can be affected
microscopy: Vascular or tissue inflammation
Fibrinoid vascular injury in some settings
Granular immune deposits in selected lesions
clinical: Examples include immune-complex glomerulonephritis and some vasculitides
Distribution depends on the antigen and host response
examTips: Deposit composition and context determine the differential.

differentials.name: Anti-basement-membrane disease
differentials.distinction: Typically has a linear rather than granular immunofluorescence pattern.

name: Type IV hypersensitivity
definition: T-cell-mediated tissue injury that is typically delayed relative to an immediate antibody-mediated response.
pathogenesis: Primed T cells recognize antigen and activate inflammatory pathways or kill target cells. Persistent stimulation can generate chronic inflammation or granulomatous responses.
gross: Contact reactions can produce inflamed skin
Persistent antigens can produce granulomatous nodules
microscopy: Lymphocytic inflammation
Epithelial injury or spongiosis in contact reactions
Macrophage granulomas in selected persistent-antigen responses
clinical: Examples include allergic contact dermatitis
The pattern depends on the target tissue and antigen
examTips: T-cell mechanism is the defining concept, not timing alone.

differentials.name: Type I hypersensitivity
differentials.distinction: Uses sensitized mast cells and IgE rather than primarily T-cell effectors.

name: Cellular hypertrophy
definition: Enlargement of cells that contributes to increased tissue or organ size.
pathogenesis: Increased workload or growth signals stimulate synthesis of cellular components. Hypertrophy can be adaptive initially and can coexist with injury or hyperplasia.
gross: The tissue or organ may be enlarged
Distribution follows the physiological or pathological stimulus
microscopy: Larger cells with increased cytoplasm
Nuclear enlargement may accompany the response
Background changes can reveal the underlying workload or injury
clinical: Can be physiological or pathological
Myocardial hypertrophy is an important example
examTips: Hypertrophy increases cell size; hyperplasia increases cell number.

differentials.name: Hyperplasia
differentials.distinction: Increases cell number rather than cell size alone.

name: Cellular hyperplasia
definition: An increase in the number of cells in a tissue in response to an appropriate or abnormal stimulus.
pathogenesis: Growth signals stimulate proliferation in tissues capable of division. Some responses diminish after removal of the stimulus, while continuing stimulation can sustain growth.
gross: Enlargement or thickening of tissue
The growth can be diffuse or nodular
microscopy: Increased numbers of the relevant cell population
Maturation can remain orderly
Architecture depends on the tissue and stimulus
clinical: Can be physiological, compensatory or pathological
May coexist with hypertrophy
examTips: Hyperplasia is not synonymous with neoplasia.

differentials.name: Neoplasia
differentials.distinction: A clonal neoplastic growth process is classified separately from an adaptive proliferation.

references.title: NCI: what is cancer, hyperplasia and dysplasia

name: Atrophy
definition: Reduction in the size of a previously developed cell, tissue or organ.
pathogenesis: Reduced workload, trophic support, perfusion or other stresses can decrease cellular components. Protein degradation and autophagy contribute, and cell loss may accompany prolonged injury.
gross: The tissue or organ becomes smaller
Fatty replacement or fibrosis may coexist
microscopy: Smaller cells with reduced cytoplasm
Residual pigment or autophagic material may accumulate
Cell loss and fibrosis can accompany chronic disease
clinical: Can follow disuse, denervation or reduced hormonal stimulation
Age-related change must be distinguished from pathological injury
examTips: Atrophy affects previously developed tissue; hypoplasia describes underdevelopment.

differentials.name: Hypoplasia
differentials.distinction: The tissue did not develop to the usual size rather than shrinking after development.

name: Reversible cell injury
definition: Cellular dysfunction and structural alteration that can recover if the injurious stimulus is removed before irreversible damage develops.
pathogenesis: Impaired energy production and membrane transport can cause ionic imbalance and water entry. Persistent or sufficiently severe damage can progress beyond the point of recovery to cell death.
gross: An affected organ may be swollen and pale
Gross changes may be subtle
microscopy: Cellular swelling and pale or vacuolated cytoplasm
Changes vary by cell type and insult
Preserved nuclei do not independently prove reversibility
clinical: Can follow hypoxia, toxins or other stressors
Clinical recovery and context inform interpretation
examTips: Do not equate every clear cytoplasmic vacuole with fat; cell swelling has a different mechanism.

differentials.name: Steatosis
differentials.distinction: Represents intracellular lipid accumulation rather than predominantly water-related swelling.

name: Granulomatous inflammation
definition: An organized inflammatory pattern dominated by aggregates of activated histiocytes, often with giant cells.
pathogenesis: Persistent material or antigen can sustain macrophage activation. T-cell-mediated immune responses and foreign-body responses can produce different granulomatous patterns.
gross: Small pale nodules may be present
Some causes produce central necrosis or larger confluent lesions
microscopy: Aggregates of epithelioid histiocytes
Multinucleated giant cells may occur
Necrosis, lymphocytes and foreign material vary with cause
clinical: Causes include infections, immune-mediated disease and foreign material
An organism may not be visible on a routine section
examTips: A granuloma is a pattern, not a diagnosis of tuberculosis or sarcoidosis by itself.

differentials.name: Granulation tissue
differentials.distinction: A vascular reparative fibroblastic tissue rather than an epithelioid-histiocyte aggregate.

stains: Acid-fast and fungal stains are selected to investigate plausible infections
Polarized light can reveal some foreign materials

name: Edema
definition: Excess fluid in an interstitial space or body cavity.
pathogenesis: Raised hydrostatic pressure, reduced plasma oncotic pressure, increased permeability, impaired lymphatic drainage or sodium retention can contribute. Several mechanisms often coexist.
gross: Swollen tissue that may pit with pressure
Pulmonary edema can produce wet heavy lungs
microscopy: Expanded interstitial spaces
Alveolar fluid can appear as pale eosinophilic material
Associated congestion or inflammation depends on cause
clinical: May be localized or generalized
Distribution helps identify the dominant mechanism
examTips: Transudative and exudative fluid accumulation have different dominant mechanisms.

differentials.name: Hemorrhage
differentials.distinction: Contains substantial extravasated blood cells rather than predominantly fluid.

name: Shock
definition: A state of inadequate effective tissue perfusion that can result in cellular hypoxia and organ dysfunction.
pathogenesis: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive or obstructive mechanisms reduce effective oxygen delivery or utilization. Persistent imbalance can trigger endothelial injury, inflammation and multiorgan failure.
gross: Findings vary with cause and duration
Affected organs can show congestion or ischemic injury
microscopy: Ischemic injury in vulnerable tissues
Acute tubular injury may occur in kidney
Microvascular thrombosis can coexist in selected settings
clinical: A physiological syndrome rather than one histological diagnosis
Sepsis is one cause, not a synonym
examTips: A tissue section alone cannot determine every shock mechanism.

differentials.name: Local ischemia
differentials.distinction: Can damage one vascular territory without systemic perfusion failure.

references.title: OpenStax: vascular homeostasis and circulatory shock

name: Nephrotic syndrome
definition: A clinical syndrome of heavy glomerular protein loss with associated systemic effects.
pathogenesis: Injury to the glomerular filtration barrier permits excessive urinary protein loss. Hypoalbuminemia, altered sodium handling and hepatic lipid responses contribute to the syndrome.
gross: Generalized soft-tissue edema may occur
There is no single syndrome-specific kidney appearance
microscopy: The pattern depends on the underlying disease
Podocyte injury may require electron microscopy
Immunofluorescence distinguishes immune-deposit patterns
clinical: Can involve edema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia
Causes and complications vary with age and context
examTips: Nephrotic describes a clinical pattern rather than one biopsy diagnosis.

differentials.name: Nephritic syndrome
differentials.distinction: Emphasizes inflammatory glomerular injury with hematuria, although overlapping presentations occur.

name: Nephritic syndrome
definition: A clinical pattern of glomerular inflammatory injury with hematuria and variable reduction in filtration.
pathogenesis: Inflammatory injury disrupts glomerular capillary integrity. Red cells enter the urinary space while reduced filtration can lead to fluid retention and azotemia.
gross: Kidneys may be swollen in acute disease
There is no single gross lesion shared by every cause
microscopy: Proliferative glomerular patterns can occur
Necrosis or crescents occur in some aggressive forms
Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy help classify the cause
clinical: Hematuria, hypertension and impaired renal function can occur
Proteinuria varies and can overlap with a nephrotic presentation
examTips: Nephritic and nephrotic features are not rigidly exclusive.

differentials.name: Nonglomerular hematuria
differentials.distinction: Arises from other urinary-tract structures without a primary inflammatory glomerular lesion.

name: Malignant neoplasia
definition: A neoplastic process capable of destructive local invasion and, in many cases, metastatic spread.
pathogenesis: Accumulated molecular alterations disturb growth control and other cellular functions. Behavior reflects both the neoplastic cells and their interaction with surrounding tissues and the host.
gross: A mass can be irregular, infiltrative, necrotic or ulcerated
Some malignancies are diffuse or grossly subtle
microscopy: Destructive invasion can establish malignancy in suitable tissues
Atypia and mitotic activity vary
Some malignant tumours are deceptively bland
clinical: Classification, grade and stage answer different questions
Diagnosis uses tissue-specific criteria
examTips: Severe atypia is not a universal definition of cancer, and blandness does not guarantee benignity.

differentials.name: Benign neoplasm
differentials.distinction: Generally lacks destructive invasion and metastatic capacity, while still being potentially locally important.

references.title: National Cancer Institute: what is cancer

name: Metastasis
definition: Spread of a malignant tumour to a noncontiguous site with formation of a secondary deposit.
pathogenesis: Tumour cells invade, enter a transport route, survive transit and establish growth at another site. Lymphatic, hematogenous and body-cavity dissemination create different patterns.
gross: Multiple organ nodules can occur
A secondary deposit can resemble or differ from the primary tumour
microscopy: A neoplastic lineage appears at a secondary anatomical site
Morphology may resemble the primary lesion
Ancillary studies and clinical imaging help assign origin
clinical: Spread affects staging and assessment
A solitary metastatic deposit is possible
examTips: A tumour within an organ is not automatically a primary tumour of that organ.

differentials.name: Synchronous primary tumour
differentials.distinction: Has an independent origin established through integrated pathological and clinical evidence.

stains: Marker panels are chosen for the specific primary-site differential

references.title: National Cancer Institute: what is cancer

name: Tissue regeneration
definition: Replacement of injured cells by the same functional cell type through proliferation of surviving cells or progenitors.
pathogenesis: Regenerative capacity depends on cell proliferative potential and preservation of the supporting framework. When injury is extensive or the framework is lost, repair increasingly relies on scar formation.
gross: Normal form may be restored after limited injury
Large injuries can leave a residual defect or scar
microscopy: Proliferation of viable cells in the injured region
Regenerative atypia can occur during repair
Architecture can normalize if the scaffold remains suitable
clinical: Regenerative potential differs among tissues
Persistent injury can prevent complete restitution
examTips: Regeneration and scar formation can occur together in one healing lesion.

differentials.name: Fibrous repair
differentials.distinction: Replaces lost functional tissue predominantly with extracellular matrix rather than equivalent functional cells.

name: Wound healing
aliases: Healing by primary and secondary intention
definition: An overlapping process of hemostasis, inflammation, tissue formation and remodeling after injury.
pathogenesis: A provisional clot and inflammatory response prepare the injured site. New vessels, fibroblasts and epithelium restore continuity while collagen is subsequently remodeled.
gross: A healing wound may have red granulation tissue
A mature scar becomes paler and less vascular
microscopy: Early clot and inflammation
Vascular granulation tissue with fibroblasts during the proliferative phase
More collagen and less cellularity with maturation
clinical: Apposed clean wounds generally require less tissue replacement than large open defects
Infection, ischemia and host factors can impair healing
examTips: Healing phases overlap; they are not rigidly separated calendar compartments.

differentials.name: Persistent ulceration
differentials.distinction: Ongoing injury prevents completion of epithelial restoration and repair.

stains: Trichrome can highlight collagen deposition

name: Keloid and hypertrophic scar
definition: Excessive scar formation; a keloid extends beyond the original wound whereas a hypertrophic scar remains within it.
