pathogenesis: Persistent fibroblastic and extracellular-matrix responses produce excessive collagen. Host susceptibility, location and the nature of injury influence the response.
gross: A raised firm scar
A keloid grows beyond the original injury boundary
microscopy: Broad densely eosinophilic collagen bundles in a typical keloid
Variable fibroblastic cellularity
Scar can replace normal cutaneous structures
clinical: Can follow surgery, burns or other injury
Clinical growth pattern helps distinguish the scar types
examTips: The relationship to the original wound is important and may not be recoverable from a section alone.

differentials.name: Dermatofibroma or other fibrous lesion
differentials.distinction: Has a different architecture and may lack a compatible scar history.

name: Chronic passive congestion
definition: Persistent tissue engorgement caused by impaired venous drainage.
pathogenesis: Elevated venous pressure impairs tissue outflow and promotes hypoxia and fluid accumulation. Repeated injury can produce hemorrhage, hemosiderin deposition and fibrosis.
gross: Affected organs may be enlarged and dark red
Congestive liver disease can produce a mottled nutmeg pattern
microscopy: Dilated blood-filled venules and sinusoids
Centrilobular hepatocyte atrophy or injury in congestive hepatopathy
Chronic changes can include fibrosis and pigment-laden macrophages
clinical: Can accompany cardiac failure or venous obstruction
The affected vascular territory guides the differential
examTips: Congestion is a passive outflow problem; hyperemia is an active increase in inflow.

differentials.name: Focal vascular lesion
differentials.distinction: May affect a localized region rather than the uniform acinar distribution of systemic congestion.

stains: Perls stain can highlight hemosiderin
Trichrome helps assess fibrosis

name: Infarction
definition: A localized area of ischemic tissue necrosis caused by loss of effective blood supply or drainage.
pathogenesis: Arterial occlusion is a common mechanism, while venous obstruction and severe hypoperfusion can also cause infarction. Collateral supply, tissue susceptibility and reperfusion influence the appearance.
gross: An infarct can be pale or hemorrhagic
A wedge-shaped lesion may follow a vascular territory
microscopy: Coagulative necrosis occurs in many solid organs
Brain infarcts typically undergo liquefaction
Inflammation and repair evolve around the dead tissue
clinical: Consequences depend on site, size and physiological reserve
An embolus does not invariably produce an infarct
examTips: Red versus pale appearance reflects the vascular and tissue context, not separate definitions of cell death.

differentials.name: Hemorrhage without infarction
differentials.distinction: Extravasated blood need not be accompanied by ischemic tissue necrosis.

name: Benign neoplasia
definition: A neoplastic proliferation without the usual invasive and metastatic properties of malignancy.
pathogenesis: Clonal growth produces a localized neoplasm with tissue-specific differentiation. Despite benign classification, location, hormonal activity or local expansion can cause significant harm.
gross: Often circumscribed rather than destructively infiltrative
A capsule can be present but is not universal
microscopy: Often resembles the mature tissue of origin
Orderly differentiation and limited atypia are common
Criteria for benignity remain tissue-specific
clinical: Can cause compression or endocrine effects
Not every benign neoplasm is clinically trivial
examTips: Circumscription alone does not prove benignity; some malignant tumours are also circumscribed.

differentials.name: Malignant neoplasm
differentials.distinction: Shows tissue-specific malignant criteria such as destructive invasion or metastatic capacity.

references.title: National Cancer Institute: what is cancer

name: Tumour grading
definition: Classification of a tumour using tissue-specific microscopic or integrated features related to differentiation and biological behavior.
pathogenesis: Different tumours use different grading systems because their predictors of behavior differ. Architectural differentiation, nuclear features, mitoses or other criteria may contribute, depending on tumour type.
gross: A gross specimen cannot reliably establish histologic grade
Heterogeneous tumours require appropriate sampling
microscopy: Degree of differentiation can contribute
Nuclear and mitotic features are assessed where relevant
Some systems incorporate specific architecture or additional findings
clinical: Provides information distinct from anatomical stage
Use the validated system for the exact tumour category
examTips: Do not transfer one tumour's grading criteria to another tumour type.

differentials.name: Tumour staging
differentials.distinction: Describes disease extent rather than the same microscopic characteristics used for grade.

name: Tumour staging
definition: Classification of the anatomical extent of a malignancy using a tumour-specific staging system.
pathogenesis: Local growth, nodal involvement and distant spread contribute to the extent of disease. Many solid-tumour systems express these components as T, N and M, but definitions vary by organ and edition.
gross: Tumour size and relationships to adjacent structures may matter
Nodes and margins must be sampled according to the specimen context
microscopy: Invasion into defined anatomical compartments can alter T category
Metastatic deposits are assessed in sampled nodes
Not every staging component is determined from histology alone
clinical: Combines pathological, imaging and clinical information as appropriate
Clinical and pathological stage can differ
examTips: Stage and grade are different variables; a small tumour can still be high grade.

differentials.name: Tumour grading
differentials.distinction: Assesses microscopic or integrated biological features rather than anatomical extent.

name: Carcinogenesis
definition: The multistep acquisition and selection of cellular alterations that enable malignant growth.
pathogenesis: Genetic and epigenetic changes affect growth signaling, cell survival, DNA maintenance and interactions with the host. Clonal selection can generate heterogeneous populations rather than one uniform tumour cell type.
gross: There is no single gross appearance shared by all carcinogenic pathways
Precursor lesions and invasive tumours can coexist
microscopy: Progressive changes can include hyperplasia, dysplasia or invasion in some tissues
Not every cancer follows the same visible precursor sequence
Morphology alone cannot identify every molecular driver
clinical: Inherited susceptibility and acquired exposures can contribute
Most acquired tumour mutations are not inherited by offspring
examTips: Cancer is genetically driven, but genetically driven does not mean every cancer is hereditary.

differentials.name: Reactive proliferation
differentials.distinction: Can be brisk and atypical but is not by itself evidence of a malignant clonal process.

references.title: National Cancer Institute: how cancer develops

name: Autoimmunity and loss of tolerance
definition: Immune reactivity against self antigens that can cause tissue injury in an autoimmune disease.
pathogenesis: Genetic susceptibility and environmental influences can impair central or peripheral tolerance. Autoantibodies, autoreactive T cells or both then contribute to organ-specific or systemic injury.
gross: Appearance depends on the target organ
Chronic damage can produce atrophy, fibrosis or altered organ size
microscopy: Inflammation can be lymphocyte-rich
Antibody or immune-complex deposits occur in some diseases
The lesion pattern depends on the mechanism and site
clinical: Autoantibody detection must be interpreted with clinical findings
Organ-specific and systemic diseases have different distributions
examTips: A positive autoantibody test is not by itself a diagnosis of clinical autoimmune disease.

differentials.name: Immune response to infection
differentials.distinction: May resemble autoimmunity in tissue but is directed against a microbial process or triggered in that context.

name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
definition: A systemic autoimmune disease with heterogeneous clinical manifestations and several mechanisms of immune-mediated tissue injury.
pathogenesis: Loss of tolerance to nuclear and other self antigens promotes autoantibody formation. Immune complexes and other immune mechanisms can damage kidney, skin, vessels, blood cells and additional tissues.
gross: Gross findings vary by organ and disease phase
Serosal inflammation or vascular lesions may occur
microscopy: Immune-complex renal patterns vary by class
Skin can show interface injury in an appropriate lesion
Vascular and other tissue changes are context-dependent
clinical: Clinical and serological integration is essential
Disease activity and organ involvement vary over time
examTips: Neither one skin biopsy nor a positive ANA establishes the entire systemic diagnosis.

differentials.name: Other autoimmune or infection-associated disease
differentials.distinction: Can share laboratory or tissue findings and requires integrated evaluation.

stains: Immunofluorescence is useful in appropriate renal or skin specimens

name: Rheumatoid arthritis
definition: A systemic autoimmune disease characterized by chronic inflammatory synovitis and potential joint destruction.
pathogenesis: Immune activation in a susceptible host sustains synovial inflammation. Proliferative inflammatory tissue and osteoclast activation damage cartilage and bone.
gross: Thickened inflamed synovium
Pannus can extend over and erode articular surfaces
microscopy: Synovial lining hyperplasia
Chronic inflammatory infiltrates and increased vascularity
Pannus-associated cartilage or bone damage in advanced lesions
clinical: Often causes persistent inflammatory polyarthritis
Extra-articular disease can occur
examTips: Pannus is proliferative inflammatory fibrovascular tissue, not a specific organism or tumour.

differentials.name: Osteoarthritis
differentials.distinction: Is primarily degenerative although secondary inflammation may occur.

name: Down syndrome
definition: A chromosomal condition caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 material, with variable developmental and medical effects.
pathogenesis: Most cases result from meiotic nondisjunction, while translocation and mosaic forms also occur. Increased dosage of chromosome 21 genes affects development and susceptibility to several disorders.
gross: Characteristic physical features vary between individuals
Congenital cardiac or other structural abnormalities may occur
microscopy: There is no single diagnostic routine tissue section
Associated lesions must be assessed in their own anatomical context
Cytogenetic testing characterizes the chromosome abnormality
clinical: Developmental effects and hypotonia are common
Certain cardiac, hematological and other risks are increased
examTips: Trisomy, translocation and mosaic mechanisms have different implications for genetic evaluation.

differentials.name: Other causes of developmental delay
differentials.distinction: Require clinical and genetic evaluation rather than diagnosis from physical appearance alone.

name: Turner syndrome
definition: A chromosomal condition in which an X chromosome is missing or structurally altered in some or all relevant cells, producing a variable phenotype.
pathogenesis: Loss or alteration of X-chromosome material changes gene dosage. Mosaicism and structural chromosome changes contribute to substantial variation among affected individuals.
gross: Short stature and gonadal underdevelopment can occur
Cardiovascular or renal structural abnormalities may be present
microscopy: Dysgenetic ovaries can be predominantly fibrous
Follicular depletion varies with the genetic pattern
Cytogenetic studies identify the chromosome findings
clinical: Ovarian insufficiency is common
Cardiovascular and other associated findings require integrated assessment
examTips: A 45,X karyotype is classic, but not every case has that karyotype in every cell.

differentials.name: Other causes of ovarian insufficiency
differentials.distinction: Need endocrine, clinical and genetic evaluation rather than a single tissue feature.

name: Klinefelter syndrome
definition: A sex-chromosome condition usually associated with an additional X chromosome and variable testicular dysfunction.
pathogenesis: An extra X chromosome alters gene dosage and gonadal development. Mosaic and other chromosome patterns contribute to variability in the clinical effects.
gross: Small firm testes are characteristic in many adults
Body proportions and secondary sexual features vary
microscopy: Seminiferous tubular atrophy or hyalinization can occur
Germ-cell depletion impairs spermatogenesis
Interstitial Leydig-cell changes may accompany gonadal dysfunction
clinical: May be detected during evaluation of infertility or hypogonadism
Some individuals have mild or unrecognized features
examTips: A phenotype does not establish the chromosome complement; cytogenetic confirmation is important.

differentials.name: Other primary testicular failure
differentials.distinction: Can share testicular atrophy and endocrine findings without the same chromosome pattern.

name: Cystic fibrosis
definition: An inherited CFTR-related disorder with abnormal epithelial ion transport and multisystem consequences.
pathogenesis: Pathogenic CFTR variants impair epithelial transport and alter the properties of secretions. Obstruction, infection and chronic inflammation progressively damage susceptible organs.
gross: Bronchiectatic airways may contain thick secretions
The pancreas can show fibrosis and cystic ductal changes
microscopy: Mucus impaction in ducts or airways
Chronic inflammatory and destructive airway changes
Pancreatic acinar loss and fibrosis in affected patients
clinical: Respiratory and digestive disease are major features
Severity and organ involvement vary by genotype and other factors
examTips: CF is not a disorder of the lung alone; connect epithelial transport to several organ patterns.

differentials.name: Other causes of bronchiectasis
differentials.distinction: Can produce similar airway destruction without a CFTR-related multisystem disorder.

name: Neurofibromatosis type 1
definition: A genetic condition with pigmentary findings, nerve-sheath tumours and other variable manifestations.
pathogenesis: Pathogenic changes affecting neurofibromin disrupt regulation of cellular signaling. Additional alterations in susceptible cells contribute to tumour development and variable organ involvement.
gross: Multiple cutaneous neurofibromas may be present
Cafe-au-lait macules and other physical findings vary with age
microscopy: Neurofibromas contain spindle cells with wavy nuclei
A mixed cellular population is embedded in collagenous or myxoid stroma
Plexiform growth follows multiple nerve fascicles in some lesions
clinical: Features can emerge over time
Some tumours have important malignant potential and require clinical evaluation
examTips: A solitary neurofibroma does not by itself establish NF1.

differentials.name: Other pigmentary or nerve-tumour syndromes
differentials.distinction: Require assessment of the complete clinical and genetic pattern.

stains: S100 and SOX10 identify Schwann-cell differentiation in suitable tissue

name: Familial hypercholesterolemia
definition: An inherited disorder associated with markedly elevated LDL cholesterol and increased risk of premature atherosclerotic disease.
pathogenesis: Variants affecting LDL uptake or related pathways impair clearance of circulating LDL. Prolonged lipid exposure promotes arterial lipid accumulation and atherosclerosis.
gross: Tendon or cutaneous xanthomas can occur
Premature atherosclerotic plaques may be extensive
microscopy: Xanthomas contain lipid-laden histiocytes
Atherosclerotic lesions show lipid accumulation and fibrous response
No single tissue appearance identifies the causal variant
clinical: Severity depends on genotype and other factors
Family history and lipid/genetic evaluation are important
examTips: Xanthomas are clues to lipid disease, not an exclusive diagnostic marker of FH.

differentials.name: Secondary hypercholesterolemia
differentials.distinction: Can elevate LDL through acquired disorders and requires clinical exclusion.

name: Vitamin A deficiency
definition: Insufficient vitamin A availability causing impaired visual-cycle and epithelial functions.
pathogenesis: Deficient intake, malabsorption or other factors reduce vitamin A availability. Impaired retinoid-dependent functions alter vision and epithelial differentiation.
gross: Ocular surface dryness can occur
Advanced ocular disease can damage the cornea
microscopy: Squamous metaplasia or keratinization can occur in susceptible epithelium
Mucus-secreting epithelial function can be impaired
The sampled site and severity determine the appearance
clinical: Night blindness is an important early clinical clue
Disease can coexist with broader nutritional problems
examTips: Separate the visual-cycle effect from the epithelial-differentiation effect when explaining the pathology.

differentials.name: Other causes of dry eye or corneal injury
differentials.distinction: Require clinical and nutritional evaluation rather than diagnosis from dryness alone.

references.title: OpenStax: nutrition, vitamins and deficiency effects

name: Rickets and osteomalacia
definition: Disorders of defective mineralization; rickets affects growing growth plates, while osteomalacia affects formed bone.
pathogenesis: Vitamin D deficiency is one cause, while phosphate disorders and other mechanisms can also impair mineralization. Unmineralized matrix accumulates and growing cartilage can become disorganized.
gross: Bone deformity can develop in a growing skeleton
Softened bone can be vulnerable to insufficiency fractures
microscopy: Excess unmineralized osteoid in osteomalacia
A widened disorganized growth plate in rickets
The cause requires biochemical and clinical evaluation
clinical: Can cause skeletal pain, deformity or fractures
Age and underlying mechanism influence the pattern
examTips: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization; osteoporosis is reduced bone amount with ordinarily preserved mineralization.

differentials.name: Osteoporosis
differentials.distinction: Predominantly reduces the quantity of normally mineralized bone rather than leaving excess unmineralized osteoid.

stains: Undecalcified bone methods assess mineralization when indicated

references.title: OpenStax: vitamin D and skeletal mineralization

name: Scurvy
definition: Clinical disease caused by vitamin C deficiency with impaired connective-tissue integrity.
pathogenesis: Vitamin C supports normal collagen maturation and other cellular functions. Deficiency weakens supporting tissues and can impair wound repair and vascular integrity.
gross: Perifollicular hemorrhages or bruising can occur
Gingival changes may develop in the appropriate context
microscopy: Hemorrhage around vulnerable small vessels
Defective connective-tissue support and repair
Bone-growth abnormalities can occur in children
clinical: Can cause bleeding, poor wound healing and constitutional symptoms
Dietary and other risk factors are important
examTips: Connect the collagen defect to capillary fragility and impaired repair rather than describing scurvy as a clotting-factor deficiency.

differentials.name: Other bleeding disorders
differentials.distinction: Can share bruising but have different hemostatic or connective-tissue mechanisms.

name: Protein-energy malnutrition
definition: A spectrum of nutritional deficiency in which inadequate energy and nutrient availability impairs body composition and function.
pathogenesis: Insufficient intake, impaired absorption, increased requirements and illness can contribute. Infection, inflammation and metabolic adaptation influence the phenotype, so the clinical forms are not explained by one nutrient alone.
gross: Muscle and fat wasting can occur
Edematous forms can mask loss of tissue mass
microscopy: Skeletal-muscle and other tissue atrophy
Fatty hepatic change can occur in edematous malnutrition
Specific findings depend on severity and coexisting deficiencies
clinical: Can impair growth, immunity and repair
Assessment integrates nutritional history and clinical findings
examTips: Avoid reducing every edematous case to isolated protein deficiency without considering the broader disease context.

differentials.name: Cachexia
differentials.distinction: Illness-associated metabolic and inflammatory wasting can coexist with nutritional deficiency but is not identical to uncomplicated starvation.

name: Bronchial asthma
definition: A heterogeneous chronic airway disorder characterized clinically by variable respiratory symptoms and expiratory airflow limitation.
pathogenesis: Airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness produce variable narrowing. Repeated injury and repair can remodel the airway wall, but inflammatory phenotypes differ among patients.
gross: Mucus plugging can obstruct airways
Hyperinflation can occur in severe episodes
microscopy: Airway mucus and goblet-cell changes
Subepithelial collagen thickening and smooth-muscle enlargement can occur
Eosinophilic inflammation is prominent in some but not all forms
clinical: A clinical and physiological diagnosis rather than a biopsy diagnosis alone
Atopic and nonatopic settings occur
examTips: Curschmann spirals and Charcot–Leyden crystals are clues in suitable material, not mandatory findings.

differentials.name: Chronic bronchitis
differentials.distinction: Has a different clinical definition and often accompanies fixed obstructive lung disease.

name: Chronic bronchitis
definition: A clinical syndrome of persistent productive cough over a defined recurring duration after other causes have been excluded.
pathogenesis: Chronic airway irritants, especially tobacco smoke, can promote mucus hypersecretion and inflammation. Small-airway remodeling can contribute to airflow obstruction, often with coexisting emphysema.
gross: Airways may contain abundant mucus
Bronchial mucosa can be congested or thickened
microscopy: Mucous-gland enlargement in larger airways
Goblet-cell metaplasia in smaller airways
Variable chronic inflammation and bronchiolar fibrosis
clinical: Classically defined by productive cough for at least three months in each of two consecutive years
The pathological changes support but do not independently establish the clinical syndrome
examTips: The Reid index is a historical morphometric measure of bronchial gland enlargement, not a universal modern diagnostic test.

differentials.name: Bronchiectasis
differentials.distinction: Has irreversible destructive airway dilation rather than mucus hypersecretion alone.

references.title: Libre Pathology: medical lung disease and chronic bronchitis

name: Diffuse alveolar damage and ARDS
definition: Diffuse alveolar damage is a pattern of acute lung injury that can accompany the clinical syndrome ARDS, but the two terms are not interchangeable.
pathogenesis: Injury to alveolar epithelium and endothelium disrupts the air–blood barrier. Protein-rich leakage and epithelial damage can progress to organization and fibrosis in some patients.
gross: Heavy congested poorly aerated lungs
Consolidation can become diffuse
microscopy: Hyaline membranes in the exudative phase
Interstitial edema and inflammatory changes
Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia and organization in later phases
clinical: Occurs with several severe pulmonary or systemic insults
Not every clinical ARDS case has DAD in a sampled tissue specimen
examTips: Hyaline membranes are a pattern of injury, not a specific diagnosis of one cause.

differentials.name: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
differentials.distinction: Predominantly reflects hydrostatic pressure rather than the same acute permeability-injury pattern.

name: Crescentic glomerulonephritis
definition: A severe glomerular-injury pattern with extracapillary crescent formation, often associated with rapidly progressive renal dysfunction.
pathogenesis: Severe capillary-wall injury allows fibrin and inflammatory signals into Bowman's space. Parietal epithelial cells and inflammatory cells form a crescent that can evolve from cellular to fibrous.
gross: Kidneys may be swollen in acute disease
Gross appearance does not determine the immune mechanism
microscopy: Crescents in Bowman's space
Capillary necrosis may coexist
Immunofluorescence can be linear, granular immune-complex, or pauci-immune
clinical: The lesion pattern requires urgent etiologic classification in clinical practice
Anti-GBM, immune-complex and pauci-immune diseases are major groups
examTips: RPGN is a clinical course; crescents are a pathological finding and need not be present in identical proportions in every case.

differentials.name: Other causes of acute kidney injury
differentials.distinction: May reduce function without the same severe extracapillary glomerular-injury pattern.

stains: Immunofluorescence is central to mechanistic classification
Fibrin stains can highlight active crescent-associated material

name: Lupus nephritis
definition: Renal involvement associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, with several glomerular and nonglomerular lesion patterns.
pathogenesis: Immune deposition and inflammatory pathways injure renal structures. The distribution and severity of lesions determine the pathological class and activity or chronicity features.
gross: There is no single class-specific gross appearance
Acute swelling or chronic scarring can occur
microscopy: Mesangial, proliferative or membranous patterns can occur
A full-house immunofluorescence pattern is a useful but not universal clue
Necrosis, crescents and chronic scarring are assessed separately
clinical: Can produce nephritic, nephrotic or mixed features
Biopsy interpretation requires clinical and serological correlation
examTips: Lupus nephritis is not one uniform microscopic picture; classification and activity are different assessments.

differentials.name: Other immune-complex glomerulonephritis
differentials.distinction: May overlap morphologically and can occasionally show a lupus-like staining pattern.

stains: Immunofluorescence and electron microscopy characterize immune deposits

name: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
definition: An inherited cystic renal disease, commonly related to PKD1 or PKD2, with progressive cyst formation and variable extrarenal manifestations.
pathogenesis: Altered polycystin-related signaling affects tubular-cell behavior. Expanding cysts distort renal architecture and can contribute to progressive loss of functioning parenchyma.
gross: Bilaterally enlarged kidneys with numerous variably sized cysts
Cysts can contain clear fluid, blood or other material
microscopy: Cysts lined by flattened or cuboidal epithelium
Intervening renal parenchyma with variable chronic damage
Fibrosis and tubular atrophy in advanced disease
clinical: Can cause hypertension, hematuria or renal impairment
Liver cysts and other extrarenal associations can occur
examTips: Multiple cysts do not by themselves prove inherited ADPKD; age, kidney size and clinical context matter.

differentials.name: Acquired cystic kidney disease
differentials.distinction: Occurs in a different chronic renal setting and often has a different overall clinical and gross context.

name: Hydronephrosis
definition: Dilation of the renal collecting system, often associated with impaired urinary drainage.
pathogenesis: Obstruction or other disturbances of drainage can increase pressure in the collecting system. Persistent pressure and associated injury can cause cortical thinning and loss of function.
gross: Dilated pelvis and calyces
Advanced cases can show marked cortical thinning
microscopy: Tubular dilation or atrophy depending on duration
Interstitial fibrosis in chronic damage
Superimposed inflammation can occur with infection
clinical: Causes include stones, outlet obstruction and tumours
Dilation requires clinical interpretation because not every dilated system reflects active obstruction
examTips: Locate the level and cause of obstruction rather than treating hydronephrosis as the final etiologic diagnosis.

differentials.name: Cystic renal disease
differentials.distinction: Produces cysts within renal tissue rather than simple dilation of the pelvicalyceal system.

name: Multinodular goiter
definition: A benign nodular enlargement of the thyroid produced by heterogeneous follicular growth and involution.
pathogenesis: Repeated cycles of growth and involution generate nodules with differing follicular activity. Iodine availability, local growth factors and other influences contribute in different settings.
gross: An enlarged multinodular thyroid
Hemorrhage, cystic change and calcification can occur
microscopy: Follicles of variable size with variable colloid
Patchy hyperplastic and involuted regions
Fibrosis, old hemorrhage or degenerative changes may be present
clinical: Can produce compressive effects or functional abnormalities
Most nodules require integrated clinical and imaging assessment
examTips: Nodular hyperplasia and a true encapsulated follicular neoplasm are different pathological categories.

differentials.name: Follicular adenoma
differentials.distinction: Usually forms a discrete encapsulated neoplasm rather than a broadly multinodular hyperplastic gland.

name: Pituitary adenoma / pituitary neuroendocrine tumour
definition: A usually indolent adenohypophyseal neuroendocrine neoplasm classified by cellular lineage and hormone-related features.
pathogenesis: A pituitary-cell clone proliferates and may secrete excess hormone. Local growth can compress normal gland or adjacent structures even when metastatic behavior is absent.
gross: A soft sellar mass
Larger lesions can show hemorrhage or cystic degeneration
microscopy: Relatively uniform neuroendocrine cells in a lineage-dependent pattern
Disruption of the normal acinar reticulin framework
Cytoplasmic staining and architecture vary by tumour type
clinical: Can present through hormone excess, hormone deficiency or mass effects
A clinically nonfunctioning lesion can still express lineage markers
examTips: Assess hormone expression and lineage rather than classifying all lesions only as acidophilic, basophilic or chromophobic.

differentials.name: Pituitary hyperplasia
differentials.distinction: Typically retains more of the normal reticulin-supported acinar arrangement.

stains: Reticulin assesses architecture
Pituitary hormones and transcription factors help establish lineage

references.title: Libre Pathology: pituitary gland and adenomas

name: Adrenal cortical adenoma
definition: A benign adrenal cortical neoplasm that may be hormonally functioning or nonfunctioning.
pathogenesis: Clonal cortical-cell proliferation forms a localized mass. Molecular pathways and hormone secretion vary among lesions.
gross: A circumscribed often yellow adrenal nodule
Lipid content and degenerative changes can alter the colour
microscopy: Cortical-type cells with clear or eosinophilic cytoplasm
Nested or trabecular growth
Assessment for malignant criteria is performed in the appropriate tumour context
clinical: May be incidental or associated with hormone excess
Functional status is established clinically and biochemically
examTips: Hormone production does not by itself distinguish benign adenoma from cortical carcinoma.

differentials.name: Adrenal cortical carcinoma
differentials.distinction: Uses integrated histological and clinical criteria; size or a single atypical feature is insufficient alone.

stains: SF1, inhibin and other markers can support cortical lineage in a panel

name: Phyllodes tumour
definition: A biphasic breast fibroepithelial tumour with a characteristic leaf-like architecture, classified as benign, borderline or malignant.
pathogenesis: The neoplastic stromal component interacts with benign epithelial elements. Stromal growth, atypia, mitotic activity and borders help determine the pathological category.
gross: A fleshy mass with cleft-like spaces
Large lesions can show necrosis or hemorrhage
microscopy: Leaf-like projections lined by benign epithelium
A relatively cellular stromal component
Stromal overgrowth, atypia and infiltrative borders vary by category
clinical: Often presents as a growing breast mass
Sampling must address tumour heterogeneity
examTips: The stroma is the main component used for grading; a benign epithelial lining does not make the entire tumour benign.

differentials.name: Fibroadenoma
differentials.distinction: Often has less prominent leaf-like architecture and a less cellular, less atypical stroma.

name: Chronic pancreatitis
definition: Persistent pancreatic injury with irreversible structural damage, fibrosis and loss of functional parenchyma.
pathogenesis: Recurrent or ongoing injury from several causes drives inflammation and fibrotic remodeling. Duct obstruction and altered secretions can sustain acinar damage.
gross: A firm fibrotic pancreas
Dilated ducts or calcifications can be present
microscopy: Acinar atrophy and loss
Fibrosis with chronic inflammation
Distorted or dilated ducts with variable intraluminal material
clinical: Can cause chronic pain, malabsorption or diabetes
Etiologies include toxic, obstructive, genetic and immune-mediated processes
examTips: Fibrosis and distorted ducts can mimic pancreatic carcinoma; assess destructive invasion and the overall distribution.

differentials.name: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
differentials.distinction: Shows invasive malignant glands and other malignant features rather than only chronic inflammatory distortion.

name: Osteoporosis
definition: Reduced bone strength related to decreased bone quantity and altered microarchitecture, with increased fracture susceptibility.
pathogenesis: An imbalance between bone resorption and formation reduces skeletal mass. Age, hormonal status, disease and medications can contribute through different mechanisms.
gross: Thin cortices and fragile bone can occur
Trabecular loss contributes to skeletal weakness
microscopy: Reduced amount and connectivity of trabecular bone
Cortical thinning or porosity
Remaining matrix is ordinarily mineralized rather than dominated by excess unmineralized osteoid
clinical: Fragility fractures may be the first presentation
Clinical evaluation assesses both bone status and secondary causes
examTips: Contrast reduced quantity of mineralized bone with impaired mineralization in osteomalacia.

differentials.name: Osteomalacia
differentials.distinction: Has defective mineralization with increased unmineralized osteoid rather than simply reduced bone amount.

references.title: Libre Pathology: bone and metabolic bone disease

name: Malaria
definition: A mosquito-borne infection caused by Plasmodium parasites, with erythrocytic stages central to blood-film diagnosis.
pathogenesis: Parasites develop through hepatic and blood stages. Erythrocyte invasion, destruction and species-dependent vascular effects produce the clinical disease.
gross: Splenic enlargement can occur
Severe disease can affect several organs
microscopy: Parasites within erythrocytes on suitable blood films
Ring forms and other stages vary by species
Pigment and tissue sequestration can be present in selected settings
clinical: Can cause febrile illness, anemia and severe organ complications
Species identification and parasite density are clinically important
examTips: A basophilic dot in a red cell is not automatically malaria; assess the full parasite morphology and sampling quality.

differentials.name: Babesiosis
differentials.distinction: Can also produce intraerythrocytic forms and requires morphological and exposure-context assessment.

stains: Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films are used for examination

name: Hemophilia A and B
definition: Inherited coagulation-factor disorders classically caused by deficient factor VIII in hemophilia A or factor IX in hemophilia B.
pathogenesis: Reduced coagulation-factor activity impairs generation of a stable fibrin clot. The common inherited forms are X-linked, although severity and clinical expression vary.
gross: Joint or deep-tissue hemorrhage can occur
Repeated hemarthroses can damage joints
microscopy: There is no unique diagnostic blood-film appearance
Affected tissues can show recent or organizing hemorrhage
Chronic joint bleeding can lead to synovial changes and pigment deposition
clinical: Deep bleeding and hemarthrosis are characteristic
Diagnosis uses the clinical history and coagulation-factor assays
examTips: A is factor VIII and B is factor IX; a tissue section does not establish the factor deficiency.

differentials.name: Von Willebrand disease
differentials.distinction: Often emphasizes mucocutaneous bleeding and involves VWF-related platelet adhesion and factor VIII biology.

name: Von Willebrand disease
definition: A bleeding disorder caused by deficient or dysfunctional von Willebrand factor.
pathogenesis: VWF supports platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII in circulation. Quantitative or qualitative defects therefore alter primary hemostasis and sometimes coagulation-factor activity.
gross: Mucosal bleeding or bruising can occur
There is no defining gross marrow lesion
microscopy: No unique routine blood-film finding establishes the disorder
Tissues can show hemorrhage
Laboratory functional and quantitative assays characterize the defect
clinical: Mucocutaneous bleeding is a common pattern
Clinical severity varies substantially among types
examTips: Type 1 is usually partial quantitative deficiency, type 2 qualitative dysfunction, and type 3 near absence of VWF.

differentials.name: Platelet-function disorder
differentials.distinction: Can produce similar bleeding and requires targeted laboratory assessment.

name: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
definition: Acute red-cell destruction associated with transfusion, most often investigated as an immune compatibility-related event.
pathogenesis: Recipient antibodies can react with transfused red-cell antigens and activate destructive immune pathways. ABO incompatibility is an important mechanism, but other antibodies and nonimmune causes of hemolysis must also be considered.
gross: Hemoglobinemia or dark urine can occur
Severe cases can have bleeding or organ injury
microscopy: No single tissue section establishes the transfusion mechanism
Hemolysis and secondary ischemic injury may be present
Microvascular fibrin thrombi can occur with associated DIC
clinical: The clinical temporal relationship and transfusion investigation are essential
Renal injury and coagulopathy can complicate severe reactions
examTips: Not every acute hemolytic reaction is ABO-mediated; investigate compatibility and alternative mechanisms.

differentials.name: Nonimmune hemolysis
differentials.distinction: Mechanical, thermal or other red-cell damage can occur without the same antibody mechanism.

references.title: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: acute haemolytic reactions

name: Transfusion-related acute lung injury
definition: An acute transfusion-associated lung-injury syndrome with noncardiogenic pulmonary edema within the defined clinical time window.
pathogenesis: Inflammatory activation of pulmonary cells and endothelium can increase vascular permeability. Antibody-related and other mechanisms may contribute in a susceptible clinical setting.
gross: Heavy edematous lungs can occur
Gross findings do not distinguish every cause of acute lung edema
microscopy: Permeability-related pulmonary edema
Acute lung injury can be present
Histology alone cannot establish the transfusion attribution
clinical: Classically develops during or within six hours of transfusion
Competing causes of acute respiratory deterioration require assessment
examTips: Differentiate permeability injury from predominantly hydrostatic overload; the clinical setting and definitions matter.

differentials.name: TACO
differentials.distinction: Predominantly reflects transfusion-associated circulatory overload rather than the same permeability mechanism.

imageQueries: transfusion related acute lung injury diagram

name: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
definition: A transfusion-associated syndrome of circulatory overload with respiratory compromise and evidence supporting hydrostatic pulmonary edema.
pathogenesis: Transfusion can exceed an individual's capacity to accommodate the added circulating volume or cardiovascular load. Increased pulmonary hydrostatic pressure promotes alveolar fluid accumulation.
gross: Wet heavy lungs can occur
Systemic signs of fluid overload may coexist
microscopy: Pulmonary edema is the dominant tissue pattern
Congestion can accompany the edema
Microscopy does not by itself determine transfusion causality
clinical: Can develop during or within the accepted post-transfusion surveillance period, often up to twelve hours
Cardiac and fluid-balance evidence helps the assessment
examTips: Hypertension can support a clinical assessment but is not present in every case.

differentials.name: TRALI
differentials.distinction: Involves predominantly permeability-related injury rather than hydrostatic overload.

name: Lead toxicity
definition: Multisystem toxicity caused by absorbed lead, with neurological, hematological, renal and other effects.
pathogenesis: Lead disrupts several cellular processes and can impair blood-cell production as well as nervous-system and renal function. The pattern depends on exposure, age and duration.
gross: There is no single defining gross organ lesion
Chronic exposure can affect multiple systems
microscopy: Basophilic stippling can appear in red cells
The stippling is not specific to lead
Organ changes vary with severity and duration
clinical: Children are particularly vulnerable to developmental neurological effects
Blood-lead measurement is central to exposure assessment
examTips: Do not diagnose lead poisoning from basophilic stippling alone; it also occurs in other disorders.

differentials.name: Other causes of basophilic stippling
differentials.distinction: Thalassemia and other disturbances of erythropoiesis can produce a similar blood-film clue.

references.title: World Health Organization: lead poisoning and health
University of Utah WebPath: basophilic stippling

name: Carbon monoxide toxicity
definition: Toxic injury caused by carbon monoxide through impaired oxygen delivery and cellular oxygen use.
pathogenesis: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and interferes with oxygen transport. Additional effects on cellular respiration contribute to injury in metabolically vulnerable organs.
gross: There may be no diagnostic gross finding
A pink-red appearance, when present, is not a reliable standalone diagnostic sign
microscopy: Hypoxic injury can affect vulnerable brain regions
Myocardial injury may occur
No single routine tissue feature independently establishes exposure
clinical: Brain and heart effects are important
Co-oximetry assesses carboxyhemoglobin, while conventional pulse oximetry can be misleading
examTips: Carboxyhemoglobin concentration does not perfectly track clinical severity or prior exposure.

differentials.name: Other hypoxic or toxic injury
differentials.distinction: Can share neurological or cardiac manifestations and requires exposure and laboratory correlation.

name: Urolithiasis
definition: Formation of calculi within the urinary tract from precipitated urinary constituents.
pathogenesis: Urinary supersaturation and the balance of promoters and inhibitors influence crystal formation. Stone composition and underlying risk factors vary among patients.
gross: Stones vary in size, colour and surface texture
Some stones form branching casts of the collecting system
microscopy: Crystalline material varies with composition
Obstruction can produce secondary tubular and interstitial injury
Infection or mucosal inflammation may coexist
clinical: Can cause pain, hematuria or obstruction
Small stones may be asymptomatic
examTips: A stone's gross shape alone does not reliably establish its chemical composition.

differentials.name: Other urinary obstruction
differentials.distinction: Tumours, strictures or outlet disease can obstruct drainage without a calculus.

name: Amoebiasis
definition: Intestinal or extraintestinal infection caused by pathogenic Entamoeba histolytica.
pathogenesis: Ingested cysts release organisms that colonize the bowel. Trophozoites can invade mucosa and vessels, producing colitis or spread to sites such as liver.
gross: Ulcerative colitis lesions can be present
Extraintestinal disease can form a liver abscess
microscopy: Trophozoites may be found in damaged mucosa or biopsy material
A typical trophozoite has one nucleus with a small central karyosome
Ingested red cells are a classic clue but are not a perfectly reliable species discriminator
clinical: Luminal infection can be asymptomatic
Invasive disease can cause dysentery or extraintestinal complications
examTips: E. histolytica and some related species overlap morphologically; molecular methods can resolve the distinction.

differentials.name: Other Entamoeba species
differentials.distinction: Some are morphologically similar but generally lack the same established pathogenic role.

stains: Stool trichrome and appropriate wet preparations show cysts or trophozoites
H&E can demonstrate organisms in tissue

name: Obesity and adipose-tissue dysfunction
definition: Abnormal or excessive adipose accumulation associated with impaired health and metabolic consequences.
pathogenesis: Genetic, environmental, behavioral and physiological influences alter energy balance and adipose biology. Adipose dysfunction and ectopic lipid accumulation can contribute to systemic disease.
gross: Increased adipose tissue with variable distribution
Associated organs can show changes such as hepatic steatosis
microscopy: Enlarged adipocytes can occur
Inflammatory cells may accompany dysfunctional adipose tissue
Organ-specific secondary lesions vary
clinical: Associated with cardiometabolic and other health risks
Risk assessment cannot be reduced to one tissue section
examTips: Adipose distribution and metabolic context matter in addition to total body size.

differentials.name: Localized adipocytic mass
differentials.distinction: A lipoma or other localized lesion is not equivalent to generalized excess adiposity.

name: Myocarditis
definition: Inflammation of myocardium with a range of infectious, immune-mediated and other causes.
pathogenesis: Direct injury or immune responses recruit inflammatory cells into myocardium. Myocyte damage and healing can impair contractile or electrical function.
gross: The heart may appear normal grossly
Severe or chronic disease can alter chamber size or wall appearance
microscopy: Interstitial inflammatory cells with a variable distribution
Myocyte injury can accompany the infiltrate
Lymphocytic, eosinophilic, giant-cell or other patterns require classification
clinical: Can present with dysfunction, arrhythmia or sudden death
Patchy disease can limit biopsy sensitivity
examTips: Inflammation alone does not identify the cause; the pattern, myocyte injury and clinical setting matter.

differentials.name: Ischemic myocardial injury
differentials.distinction: Can produce inflammation after necrosis and must be separated using distribution and other evidence.

name: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
definition: Diabetes caused by severe pancreatic beta-cell loss, usually through autoimmune mechanisms.
pathogenesis: Genetic susceptibility and immune responses contribute to beta-cell destruction. Progressive loss of insulin-producing capacity disrupts glucose and broader fuel metabolism.
gross: The pancreas may have no distinctive gross lesion
Longstanding disease can produce complications in several organs
microscopy: Islet beta-cell depletion
Insulitis can be seen in suitable early-stage material but is not universal
Late pancreatic sections may not reveal the initiating immune process
clinical: Often develops in younger people but can occur at other ages
Clinical and biochemical testing establishes diabetes and its type
examTips: Absence of insulitis in a late specimen does not exclude type 1 diabetes.

differentials.name: Other diabetes types
differentials.distinction: May involve insulin resistance, genetic defects or pancreatic injury rather than the same autoimmune beta-cell loss.

stains: Insulin immunostaining assesses beta cells in appropriate research or diagnostic material

name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
definition: Diabetes associated with insulin resistance and inadequate compensatory insulin secretion.
pathogenesis: Genetic susceptibility and environmental or physiological factors contribute to insulin resistance. Beta-cell dysfunction progressively limits compensation and promotes sustained hyperglycemia.
gross: No single gross pancreatic finding establishes the diagnosis
Vascular and other organ complications can become prominent
microscopy: Islet amyloid may occur
Beta-cell mass and architecture can be altered
Microvascular and large-vessel lesions develop in affected organs
clinical: Can be clinically silent before detection
Complications involve kidney, retina, nerves and the cardiovascular system
examTips: Islet amyloid is associated with type 2 disease but is not required in every specimen.

differentials.name: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
differentials.distinction: Usually centers on immune-associated beta-cell loss rather than the same initial insulin-resistance pattern.

stains: Congo red can demonstrate islet amyloid when present

references.title: Libre Pathology: amyloid including pancreatic deposits

name: Acute pyelonephritis
definition: Acute infection-associated inflammation of renal parenchyma and the collecting system.
pathogenesis: Ascending infection is a common route, although blood-borne infection can also involve kidney. Host factors, reflux or impaired drainage can promote renal involvement.
gross: A swollen kidney can contain patchy suppurative foci
Pelvicalyceal inflammation may be present
microscopy: Neutrophilic tubulointerstitial inflammation
Tubulitis and neutrophils in tubular lumens
Microabscesses or parenchymal destruction in severe disease
clinical: Can present with fever, flank pain and urinary findings
Clinical microbiology identifies the infectious cause
examTips: A neutrophilic interstitial pattern suggests a differential and does not independently identify the organism.

differentials.name: Other acute tubulointerstitial nephritis
differentials.distinction: Can cause renal dysfunction and inflammation without the same suppurative infectious context.

stains: Organism stains are selected when indicated and do not replace culture

references.title: Libre Pathology: acute pyelonephritis and medical kidney disease

name: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
definition: An inherited fibrocystic disorder with renal collecting-duct disease and associated congenital hepatic fibrosis.
pathogenesis: PKHD1-related dysfunction affects epithelial structures in kidney and biliary development. Disease severity varies, with different proportions of renal and hepatic involvement over time.
gross: Kidneys can be bilaterally enlarged with a relatively smooth surface
Fine radially arranged cystic spaces can involve the parenchyma
microscopy: Dilated collecting ducts in a radial pattern
Variable renal parenchymal injury
Associated liver disease can show ductal-plate malformation and portal fibrosis
clinical: Severe disease can present early in life
Surviving patients can develop important renal and portal-hypertensive complications
examTips: ARPKD and ADPKD are distinct disorders, not simply different ages of the same disease.

differentials.name: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
differentials.distinction: Usually has a different genetic mechanism and gross cyst distribution, although clinical timing can overlap.

imageQueries: autosomal recessive polycystic kidney gross pathology

name: Aortic dissection
definition: Separation of layers within the aortic wall by blood, creating a dissecting channel.
pathogenesis: An entry tear and underlying wall susceptibility commonly permit blood to track through the media. Extension can compromise branches, the valve region or the outer wall.
gross: A channel within the aortic wall may be visible
An intimal tear and true and false lumens can be identified in suitable specimens
microscopy: Hemorrhagic separation within the media
Variable medial degeneration or other underlying wall changes
Elastic-fibre disruption can be assessed with an appropriate stain
clinical: Can cause acute pain, malperfusion or rupture
Extent and involvement of the ascending aorta have major clinical implications
examTips: Dissection is a wall-separation process and is not synonymous with an ordinary atherosclerotic aneurysm.

differentials.name: Aortic aneurysm without dissection
differentials.distinction: Represents dilation of the vessel and need not contain a blood-filled dissecting channel.

stains: Elastic stains help assess medial architecture

name: HIV-associated immunodeficiency and AIDS
definition: Acquired immune dysfunction caused by HIV infection, with advanced disease associated with characteristic opportunistic and neoplastic complications.
pathogenesis: HIV infection and associated immune activation progressively disturb immune function, especially CD4 T-cell-mediated responses. The resulting susceptibility to particular infections and tumours varies with the degree of immune impairment.
gross: Lymphadenopathy can occur in some phases
Organ lesions depend on associated infections or neoplasms
microscopy: Lymphoid tissue can show reactive changes or depletion depending on the disease context
Opportunistic organisms produce site-specific tissue patterns
Associated lymphoid or vascular neoplasms require their own diagnostic assessment
clinical: A positive tissue pattern is not a substitute for virological diagnosis
Advanced immune dysfunction has systemic consequences
examTips: Identify both the immune context and the specific lesion; not every abnormality in a person with HIV is caused directly by the virus.

differentials.name: Other acquired immunodeficiency
differentials.distinction: Drugs, malignancy and other conditions can produce overlapping susceptibility patterns.

stains: Special stains and lineage markers are chosen for the suspected secondary lesion

name: Severe combined immunodeficiency
definition: A group of inherited disorders with severe impairment of T-cell function and variable defects in other lymphocyte compartments.
pathogenesis: Different genetic defects disrupt immune-cell development, signaling or survival. The precise B-cell and NK-cell phenotype varies, while severe cellular immune failure also impairs effective antibody responses.
gross: Lymphoid organs may be poorly developed
Severe infections can produce prominent secondary lesions
microscopy: Hypoplastic lymphoid tissue can be present
Thymic lymphocyte depletion or abnormal development depends on the form
Infection-related tissue patterns vary with the organism
clinical: Often presents early with serious or unusual infections
Immunophenotyping and genetic evaluation characterize the disorder
examTips: SCID is a group of diseases; do not assume every case has identical B-cell or NK-cell counts.

differentials.name: Other primary or acquired immunodeficiency
differentials.distinction: Can produce serious infection but has a different immunological and genetic profile.
